untested.label: No direct human tinnitus evidence found
untested.mean: No studies testing this treatment directly in people with tinnitus were found in our search. Some entries have animal research, or evidence from related drugs or conditions — always shown separately.

early.label: Early human evidence
early.mean: Small or uncontrolled studies in people with tinnitus. An early hint, not a conclusion.

controlled.label: Controlled, not yet confirmed
controlled.mean: At least one controlled trial, not yet repeated by an independent research team.

nosham.label: Many studies, but limited placebo or sham evidence
nosham.mean: There may be many studies, but adequate placebo or sham comparisons are limited. Without them, expectations and other effects can be difficult to separate from treatment effects.

mixed.label: Mixed or conflicting results
mixed.mean: Controlled studies disagree with each other.

nobenefit.label: Tested in controlled trials without showing benefit
nobenefit.mean: Available controlled evidence did not show a clear benefit over placebo or the comparison treatment.

done.note: This trial has finished. It is not ongoing research. No results were posted on the registry and no peer-reviewed publication was found in our search.

unknown.label: STATUS UNKNOWN — NO PUBLIC RESULTS FOUND
unknown.note: The registry record has not been kept up to date, so it is not known whether this trial finished. No results or publication were found in our search. It is not counted as research underway.

pub.label: COMPLETED — RESULTS PUBLISHED
pub.note: This trial has finished and its results are published; they are described in the evidence sections of this card.

term.label: TERMINATED — NO PUBLIC RESULTS FOUND
term.note: This trial was stopped early. It is not ongoing research. No results were posted and no publication was found in our search.

rc.label: RECRUITMENT COMPLETE — NO PUBLIC RESULTS FOUND

susp.label: SUSPENDED — NO PUBLIC RESULTS FOUND

mismatch.label: COMPLETED — PUBLICATION DOES NOT MATCH REGISTRATION

notin.label: COMPLETED — NO PUBLIC TINNITUS RESULTS

ended.label: ENDED (EU REGISTER) — NO PUBLIC RESULTS FOUND
ended.note: The EU trial register lists this trial as ended in January 2026; ClinicalTrials.gov has not been updated and still says “active, not recruiting.” No results were found. T.name: Supplement formulas sold online
T.alt: Quietum Plus, Cortexi, SonoVive, Silencil, Tinnitus 911, Synapse XT, Sonus Complete
T.desc: Multi-ingredient capsules and drops sold online as “tinnitus relief” formulas, usually through advertising and affiliate websites.
human: No studies of these products found in our search
T.best: None found in our search

gl.text: Applies to dietary supplements as a group (these products are dietary supplements; no guideline names these brands). AAO-HNSF (2014) recommends against “Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, or other dietary supplements”; European (2019) “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; German (2021) food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.”

T.tells: No study of any of these branded formulas in people with tinnitus was found in our search. Their claims usually rely on studies of individual ingredients or on testimonials.
facts: Claims seen include large “relief” percentages and eliminating tinnitus; no product-level study supporting them was found in our search.

The US Federal Trade Commission has taken action over tinnitus claims for other supplement products (case 1:20-cv-21622, 2020). We found no action against these specific brands (the FTC’s own site search was unavailable).
Tinnitus guidelines recommend against dietary supplements for persistent tinnitus in general; none names these brands.
Brands are listed as text only, in one card, so the page does not become a product catalogue.
src: Review of tinnitus supplements marketed online

T.name: Grey-market peptides
T.alt: BPC-157, ARA-290 (cibinetide), Semax, Selank
T.desc: Peptides sold online, mainly as “research chemicals,” and promoted for “healing” or “nerve repair,” including for tinnitus. Semax and Selank are licensed medicines in Russia; none of the four is FDA-approved.
human: No human tinnitus studies of any of the four found in our search
Semax: 1 Russian report where it was one of five treatments given together
T.best: None found for any single peptide (no animal ear or tinnitus studies either)
T.tells: No study of these peptides in people with tinnitus was found in our search, and no animal study of the ear or of tinnitus-like behaviour either. In one Russian report, Semax was one of five treatments given together to people with noise-related hearing loss and tinnitus, so its own effect cannot be separated.
facts: FDA says it lacks sufficient information to know whether BPC-157 or Semax “would cause harm” in people.
Russian medical databases could only be partly searched.
src: FDA bulk drug substances page (22 Apr 2026); FDA advisory committee briefings (11 May 2026)

parts.e: No ear, hearing or tinnitus study found. Not approved anywhere (US FDA review). Named on the 2026 anti-doping list.
Investigational; small trials in nerve pain from other diseases. No ear study found.
Licensed prescription medicine in Russia (not for hearing). One report gave it with four other treatments; its own effect cannot be separated.
Licensed medicine in Russia for anxiety. No ear study found.

T.name: PRP ear injections
T.alt: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP), PRP injections through the eardrum, “regenerative” clinic injections
T.desc: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injected through the eardrum — one of several clinic injections marketed to repair or regenerate the inner ear.
human: 4 small reports measured tinnitus — none randomized or placebo-controlled
The only comparison (50 people, not randomized) found tinnitus scores similar to steroid injections
T.best: A non-randomized comparison with steroid injections (50 people)
T.qual: Very low certainty: 4 small reports measured tinnitus — none randomized or placebo-controlled; the only comparison (with steroid injections) found no difference
T.tells: PRP injections through the eardrum have four small reports that measured tinnitus. The only comparison found tinnitus scores similar to steroid injections, and none used a placebo.
src: Asghar AM. Mediterr J Med Med Sci 2026

T.name: Stem-cell, exosome & secretome injections
T.alt: Stem cells, “exosomes,” extracellular vesicles, secretome, cord-blood or bone-marrow cells, “regenerative” clinic injections
T.desc: Clinic injections of stem cells, exosomes or secretome, marketed to repair or regenerate the inner ear and offered in several countries.
human: No human tinnitus studies found
Small hearing-loss studies measured hearing only; one vesicle study enrolled people with tinnitus but did not measure it
T.best: No study in people with tinnitus found
T.tells: No study of stem-cell, exosome or secretome injections in people with tinnitus was found in our search. The nearest human studies, in hearing loss, measured hearing only. Two registered sudden-hearing-loss trials of vesicles plan a tinnitus questionnaire as a secondary measure.

T.name: Ketamine & esketamine
T.alt: IV ketamine infusion or injections, ketamine clinics, esketamine, Spravato (esketamine nasal spray), AM-101 (esketamine ear gel — a different formulation)
T.desc: Ketamine infusions offered by clinics and promoted to “reset” tinnitus. Esketamine nasal spray (Spravato) and the esketamine ear gel AM-101 are shown separately.
human: No published tinnitus results for ketamine
A 42-person ketamine study in people with tinnitus has not reported its tinnitus outcomes
T.best: None published for ketamine
T.qual: One study in people with tinnitus has not published its tinnitus results; a different esketamine ear-gel formulation (AM-101) showed no benefit in Phase III trials and is covered elsewhere
T.tells: No published result shows ketamine infusions affecting tinnitus. A registered ketamine study in people with tinnitus planned tinnitus questionnaires but has posted only brain-chemistry results. Short-lived tinnitus has been reported as a side effect of ketamine in depression trials.

T.name: Psilocybin & other psychedelics
T.alt: Psilocybin, magic mushrooms, psilocybin retreats, other classic psychedelics (LSD, DMT, 5-MeO-DMT); MDMA shown separately
T.desc: Psilocybin or other classic psychedelics (including retreats), promoted to “reset” tinnitus. MDMA, a different drug, is shown separately.
human: No human tinnitus studies of psilocybin or other classic psychedelics found
MDMA (a different drug): 1 small placebo-controlled crossover — similar to placebo overall
T.best: Psilocybin: none. MDMA (a different drug): a small placebo-controlled crossover (13 people reported)
T.qual: Accurate for psilocybin and other classic psychedelics. MDMA (a different drug) was tested in 1 small placebo-controlled study — similar to placebo overall
T.tells: No published result shows psilocybin or other classic psychedelics affecting tinnitus. MDMA, a different drug, gave results similar to placebo overall in one very small trial. Some people report tinnitus after psychedelic use.

T.name: Kv7 potassium-channel drugs (in development)
T.alt: Retigabine (ezogabine) and laboratory analogues, flupirtine, azetukalner (XEN1101), opakalim (BHV-7000)
T.desc: Experimental and older drugs discussed as future tinnitus treatments. Kv7 drugs open potassium channels in nerve cells. AC102, a different kind of drug (not a Kv7 drug), has its own card.
human: No human tinnitus studies of the newer drugs
Flupirtine: 1 small uncontrolled study (no benefit) · retigabine: 1 online user survey
T.best: Animal studies (prevention design); 1 small uncontrolled human study of flupirtine
T.qual: Accurate for the newer Kv7 drugs. Flupirtine (an older related drug) has 1 small uncontrolled human study that found no benefit
T.tells: In animals, several of these drugs reduced tinnitus-like behaviour when given shortly after loud noise — preventing tinnitus rather than treating it. The only human tinnitus study (flupirtine, 24 people, no comparison group) found no benefit. No tinnitus trial of the newer drugs was found in our search.
T.com: One laboratory Kv7-compound study had co-authors employed by the compound’s supplier (SciFluor). A 2002 patent application for flupirtine in tinnitus (individual inventor) has lapsed. The companies developing the newer drugs (Xenon; Biohaven, licensed to SK Biopharmaceuticals) have no tinnitus programmes.

T.name: AC102 (in development)
T.alt: AC102 middle-ear gel injection (AudioCure Pharma)
T.desc: An experimental drug discussed as a future tinnitus treatment. AC102 is a small molecule injected into the middle ear as a gel. It is a different kind of drug from the Kv7 potassium-channel drugs (not a Kv7 drug), which have their own card.
human: No human tinnitus studies of AC102
Its only patient trial is in sudden hearing loss, with hearing outcomes (ended in the EU in January 2026; no results yet)
T.best: One animal study (prevention design)
T.qual: Its only patient trial is in sudden hearing loss; tinnitus was recorded only as an exploratory rating scale
T.tells: In gerbils, AC102 given right after loud noise reduced tinnitus-like behaviour — preventing tinnitus rather than treating it. That study was funded by the company developing AC102. Its only patient trial is in sudden hearing loss, with hearing outcomes; no tinnitus trial of AC102 was found in our search.
T.com: The only AC102 tinnitus study was funded by the company developing it (AudioCure Pharma), and company employees are co-authors.

T.name: IV NAD+ drips & NAD+ injections
T.alt: NAD+ infusions or injections
T.desc: NAD+ drips or injections offered by clinics, marketed for “brain” health, longevity and recovery. NAD+ precursor supplements (NR, NMN, nicotinamide) have their own card.
human: No studies of NAD+ drips in people with tinnitus found
Related: 1 sudden-hearing-loss trial of NAD+ injections (tinnitus a side-measure)
T.best: Indirect only (hearing-loss trial)
T.qual: NAD+ injections were tested in sudden hearing loss, with tinnitus only as a side-measure
T.tells: NAD+ drips have not been tested in people with tinnitus. The closest evidence is a small sudden-hearing-loss trial of low-dose NAD+ injections, where tinnitus was a side-measure with mixed results.
T.com: The hearing-loss trial was funded by Knature Biopharmaceutical Co. Ltd. and used an NAD+ injection made by Kaifeng Knature Pharmaceutical (both named in the paper); the authors declared no conflicts. The IV NAD+ tolerability data were produced or funded by NAD+ infusion providers.

T.name: NAD+ precursor supplements (NR, NMN, nicotinamide)
T.alt: Nicotinamide riboside (NR), nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), nicotinamide (vitamin B3)
T.desc: NAD+-boosting supplements (NR, NMN) promoted for nerve “repair,” and nicotinamide, another NAD+ precursor. IV NAD+ drips and NAD+ injections have their own card.
human: No studies of NR or NMN in people with tinnitus found — an NMN trial is recruiting
Nicotinamide: 1 placebo trial (1987, 48 people) — no benefit
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial of nicotinamide (1987) — no benefit; none for NR or NMN
T.qual: Accurate for NR and NMN (an NMN trial is recruiting). Nicotinamide was tested once against placebo in tinnitus (1987) — no benefit
T.tells: NR and NMN have not been tested in people with tinnitus; a placebo-controlled NMN trial in tinnitus is recruiting in Japan. Nicotinamide, another NAD+ precursor, was tested against placebo in a 1987 trial that found no benefit.
T.com: The tablets for the NMN tinnitus trial are supplied by Mitsubishi Corporation Life Sciences (trial registry), which also funded earlier NMN hearing studies by the same research group.

gl.text: Class-level only — applies to dietary supplements as a group; NR, NMN and nicotinamide are not named, and no guideline evaluated them. European (2019) “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; German (2021) food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.”

T.name: Molecular hydrogen (H₂)
T.alt: Hydrogen inhalation, hydrogen water, H₂
T.desc: Hydrogen gas breathed in through a nasal tube, or hydrogen dissolved in drinking water, promoted as an antioxidant for the ear.
human: 1 small study · 40 people
recent-onset tinnitus
T.best: Small randomized study, no placebo
T.tells: One small study in China found more improvement when people with recent-onset tinnitus inhaled hydrogen alongside a standard medication. It had no placebo, no independent replication was found in our search, and it tested inhaled hydrogen — not hydrogen water.

T.name: Lipo-Flavonoid
T.alt: Bioflavonoid (eriodictyol) with B vitamins and vitamin C
T.desc: A widely sold bioflavonoid-and-vitamin supplement marketed for “ear ringing.”
human: 2 studies · about 90 people
40 in a randomized trial (as the comparison); 51 survey completers
T.best: Randomized trial in which it was the comparison treatment — no placebo test found

gl.text: Class-level: guidelines recommend against dietary supplements as a group (AAO-HNSF 2014; European 2019; German 2021 “to be omitted”, strong). No guideline names lipoflavonoids in a recommendation statement, but the European and German guidelines list lipoflavonoids, in the supporting text of those recommendations, among supplements for which efficacy evidence “does not exist” / “is not available”.

T.com: The open-label survey was “funded by and the product was provided by Clarion Brands, makers of the Lipo-Flavonoid® commercial product” (stated in the paper). The “#1 ENT recommended” claim rests on an unpublished 2018 manufacturer survey (“data on file”).
T.tells: No placebo-controlled test of Lipo-Flavonoid for tinnitus was found in our search. In the only randomized study it was the comparison treatment, and none of the 16 people who finished that arm showed a decrease on the tinnitus questionnaires.
facts: The “#1 ENT recommended” claim comes from an unpublished manufacturer survey of how often doctors recommend it — not a test of whether it works.
In the manufacturer-funded survey, about 7% of people given the product completed it (51 of 719; our calculation).

T.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
T.alt: NAC
T.desc: An antioxidant promoted to protect hearing and reduce tinnitus. Sold as a supplement in the US; a prescription medicine in the UK and some other countries.
human: 2 case reports · 2 people
plus prevention studies in people without established tinnitus
T.best: Two single-patient reports
T.tells: NAC has not been tested as a treatment for established tinnitus in any controlled trial found in our search. In one of two single-patient reports, tinnitus eased while depression also lifted; in the other, NAC alone had not helped. Studies of NAC protecting hearing are a different question.
facts: A placebo-controlled trial of NAC during ear surgery found no effect on tinnitus, but it tested protection, not treatment.
UK prescribing information lists tinnitus as an uncommon side effect of oral NAC.
T.com: In one of the two case reports, a co-author holds equity in a company that licensed the experimental drug given alongside NAC, and another co-author is a vice president of the company that supplied it (declared in the paper).

T.name: Radiofrequency & nerve-block procedures
T.alt: Pulsed radiofrequency, nerve blocks in the neck (not stellate ganglion block), cervical nerve-root infiltration, occipital-nerve block, cervical plexus block, radiofrequency lesion of the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion, face and ear nerve blocks
T.desc: Radiofrequency treatments and local-anaesthetic injections around neck nerves, offered by some pain and ENT clinics.
human: About 24 reports (about 11 radiofrequency, about 13 nerve-block)
all uncontrolled; over half of participants from one Dutch clinic
T.best: Uncontrolled series (best reported: a prospective series of 30 people)
T.tells: Several different procedures are grouped here, and each has only uncontrolled evidence. Most radiofrequency data come from one clinic, and the first independent series found no change in tinnitus handicap. No study comparing any of these procedures with a sham procedure was found in our search.

T.name: Huneke neural therapy
T.alt: “Neural therapy” (Huneke), neural therapy after Huneke, procaine or lidocaine injections at skin segments, trigger points, scars and nerve ganglia
T.desc: Repeated small injections of local anaesthetic (procaine or lidocaine) at skin segments, trigger points, scars and nerve ganglia, offered by some ENT and complementary-medicine practices.
human: 1 series (96 people, 1983) · 1 case report
no comparison group; the series described its results only in words
T.best: Uncontrolled series from 1983 (96 people; results described only in words)
T.qual: Based on 1 old uncontrolled series and 1 case report; a small registered trial is listed as not yet recruiting
T.tells: The evidence is one uncontrolled series from 1983, with results described only in words, and one case report with dental treatment at the same time. No study comparing neural therapy with a sham procedure was found in our search. A small randomized trial is registered but not yet recruiting, and its planned dates have passed.

T.name: Upper-cervical chiropractic & neck manipulation
T.alt: Atlas / C1 adjustment, spinal manipulation, upper-cervical chiropractic
T.desc: Neck adjustments promoted as correcting a “root cause” of tinnitus.
human: About a dozen small reports · about 60 people
all in people with neck problems
T.best: Retrospective series (neck manipulation by physicians)
T.tells: The evidence is case reports and one retrospective series, in which only 10% of 47 people with neck-related tinnitus improved. No study tested manipulation in tinnitus generally. An association between neck manipulation and rare artery tears has been reported; causality has not been established.
facts: This is different from physiotherapy for jaw- or neck-related tinnitus, which has its own page.
src: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association

T.name: Vinpocetine & piracetam
T.alt: Cavinton
T.desc: Circulation and “brain-boosting” medicines widely used for ear noise in Russia and neighbouring countries.
human: About 7 studies · several hundred people
most participants were not given either drug
T.best: Open studies (vinpocetine); 2 small randomized comparisons with other medicines (piracetam)
T.tells: These are two different drugs with separate evidence. No placebo-controlled trial of either for tinnitus was found in our search. Vinpocetine studies were mostly open; two small randomized studies of piracetam, both after sudden hearing loss or noise injury, found no difference from other medicines.

parts.ml: Tested in people — no placebo comparison of vinpocetine alone
parts.e: 5 studies: open studies reported improvement; in a saline-controlled programme after acute noise injury (1986), adding vinpocetine gave no extra benefit.

parts.ml: Tested in people — randomized vs other medicines
parts.e: 2 randomized studies compared with other medicines (147 people, in sudden hearing loss or noise injury): no difference from the comparison.

a: Russia (2016; archived by the Russian Ministry of Health in May 2021 because its validity period expired — no current Russian tinnitus guideline was found)
Recommended vinpocetine for suspected blood-flow-related inner-ear disorders — at its lowest grade.
b: Advise against drug treatment for tinnitus in general (not naming vinpocetine or piracetam).

facts: Vinpocetine’s product information in Russia and Hungary lists ear noise or tinnitus as an approved use; no piracetam label checked does.
Russian and Chinese medical databases could only be partly searched.

T.name: Antinitus patch
T.alt: “Fractal light” patch
T.desc: An adhesive patch described by its maker as a light-based “biomodulator.”
human: 1 placebo-controlled trial · 82 people
plus a small pilot and manufacturer surveys
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial (82 people), run by the manufacturer
T.nop: Independent trial (NCT07731230, 91 enrolled): completed February 2021 and first registered in July 2026; no results posted and no publication found in our search.
T.tells: In the only published placebo-controlled trial (82 people, run by the manufacturer), the main measure — annoyance after 3 weeks — did not differ from placebo. One secondary result at week 7 favoured the patch; handicap scores did not differ. Sweden’s medical products agency issued a marketing ban in 2018, which the company appealed.
facts: The Swedish ban is recorded in a government report and identified as Antinitus in the company’s own announcement; the final court outcome is known only from secondary sources.
An independent trial was completed in 2021 and first registered in 2026; no results found in our search.
T.qual: Based on 1 placebo-controlled trial — its main measure was not met
T.com: Documented manufacturer conduct: Sweden’s stock-exchange market surveillance describes the placebo trial as one “the Company conducted”; company press releases call the studies “our study programme”; the earlier pilot was registered by Akloma Bioscience AB (industry sponsor). The published papers contain no funding or conflict-of-interest statements.

T.name: Botulinum toxin (Botox)
T.alt: Botox injections into jaw or neck muscles
T.desc: Injections into jaw or neck muscles, offered for tinnitus linked to muscle tension.
human: 1 small controlled trial · 30 people
plus case reports; 1 completed trial with no public results
T.best: Small placebo-controlled crossover trial (30 people, 2005)
T.nop: University of Minnesota trial (NCT05650645, 41 people): completed 29 December 2025; no results posted and no publication found in our search.
T.tells: In one small placebo-controlled crossover trial (2005), more people rated themselves improved after the toxin than after saline, but other measures did not differ from placebo, and no repeat study was found in our search. A 100-person placebo-controlled trial is underway in Norway.

a: Tinnitus linked to jaw/neck muscles (this card)
b: Clicking tinnitus from muscle spasm (a different condition)
Case series only; kept separate so the two are not confused.

facts: Regulatory warning: all botulinum toxin products carry a class-wide US boxed warning about spread of the toxin effect (FDA labels).
T.com: A University of Minnesota page states that the lead investigator’s botulinum-toxin tinnitus research is funded by a grant from Merz Pharma, maker of Xeomin (the drug in the current trial); the trial registry lists no collaborator, so a link to this specific trial is not documented. The authors of a 2026 scoping review declare affiliations with aesthetic-medicine companies. For the 2005 trial, we could not read the paper’s funding statement.

T.name: Migraine-medicine combinations (“cochlear migraine”)
T.alt: Nortriptyline with topiramate, verapamil with paroxetine, migraine-prevention medicines, otologic migraine, cochlear migraine, “cochlear migraine” medication protocols
T.desc: Pairs of migraine-prevention medicines prescribed on the theory that some tinnitus is a form of migraine (“cochlear migraine”).
human: 1 placebo-controlled trial · 78 people
not selected for migraine — about 1 in 4 had a migraine history
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial (3 groups, 8 weeks)
T.com: The trial’s senior author and registry lead discloses that he “is an advisor and holds equity in NeuroMed Care LLC, Elinava Technologies, and Cactus Medical LLC” (trial publication). NeuroMed’s web pages, written by him, promote this approach.
T.tells: In the one placebo-controlled trial, the migraine-medicine groups did not improve significantly more than placebo on the main tinnitus measure. The trial did not select people with migraine. Two further trials are registered; neither has a placebo group.
facts: Improvements reported by the clinic come from within-group changes, not the comparison with placebo.
These medicines have known side effects; the trial’s side-effect data were not extracted in our review.
src: Abouzari M, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2025
T.qual: Based on 1 small placebo-controlled trial — too small and short to rule out a modest effect

gl.text: Class-level only: the US (AAO-HNSF 2014) guideline recommends against antidepressants and anticonvulsants for routine treatment of persistent tinnitus — this covers nortriptyline, paroxetine and topiramate, not verapamil; the German (2021) guideline says drugs for chronic tinnitus are “to be avoided” (strong recommendation). No guideline names “cochlear migraine” protocols or these combinations.

T.name: Coenzyme Q10
T.alt: CoQ10, ubiquinone
T.desc: An antioxidant supplement promoted for tinnitus loudness.
human: 2 studies · 70 people
+2 registered placebo trials with no results found
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial (50 people), added to an antidepressant
T.tells: One small placebo-controlled trial (50 people, 6 weeks, taken alongside an antidepressant in both groups) reported lower tinnitus handicap scores. It was registered after recruitment began, some reported outcomes were not registered, and no independent repeat was found in our search.
facts: An earlier uncontrolled study found no overall effect.
A trial in Belgium (NCT02353650) is registered with status “unknown”; no results were found in our search.

gl.text: Applies to dietary supplements as a group — CoQ10 is not named in any guideline we checked. AAO-HNSF (2014) recommends against “… other dietary supplements”; European (2019) “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; German (2021) food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.”

T.com: One registered placebo-controlled trial (EudraCT 2008-002369-29) was sponsored by MSE Pharmazeutika GmbH, the marketing-authorisation holder of the CoQ10 product tested; no results were found. The published trial was funded by a public university and its authors declare no conflicts of interest.

T.name: Herbal products studied in Iran
T.alt: Neurotec (tansy, nettle, rose hip), nanocurcumin, a traditional herbal tea, bitter almond oil ear drops
T.desc: Four different herbal products — a tansy, nettle and rose-hip capsule (Neurotec), nanocurcumin capsules, a traditional herbal tea and bitter almond oil ear drops — each tested for tinnitus in one trial in Iran.
human: 4 trials · about 370 people analysed
4 different products; 3 more registered trials without results
T.best: Placebo-controlled trials — one each for three of the products
T.tells: Four different products, each tested once. Neurotec and a herbal tea did better than placebo on handicap scores at the end of treatment, in trials with important weaknesses. Nanocurcumin did not differ from placebo on its main measure, and almond ear drops added nothing to standard treatment. None has been repeated.

parts.e: 150 randomized, 103 analysed, 3 months: handicap and rating scores, including loudness, lower than placebo at 3 months; hearing unchanged. Registered after recruitment ended; the manufacturer supplied the placebo.

parts.ml: Placebo-controlled trial — no difference on main measure
parts.e: 62 people, 21 days: handicap scores did not differ from placebo at the end; the authors concluded it was not effective.
144 randomized: handicap score better than placebo at 56 days only; severity rating no different.
69 people: adding the drops to standard treatment made no difference.

T.qual: Differs by product: Neurotec and the herbal tea — controlled, not yet confirmed; nanocurcumin and the ear drops — no benefit shown

T.name: MemoVigor 2
T.alt: MemoVigor 2
T.desc: A multi-ingredient supplement (containing ginkgo, B vitamins and other ingredients) that has been tested against placebo.
human: 1 placebo-controlled trial
240 randomized · 204 analysed
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial

gl.text: Applies to dietary supplements as a group — MemoVigor 2 is not named in any guideline we checked. AAO-HNSF (2014) recommends against “Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, or other dietary supplements”; European (2019) “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; German (2021) food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.” None of these guidelines assessed this trial.

T.com: The manufacturer (EUROPHARMA, Italy) donated the tablets and the placebo.
T.tells: MemoVigor 2 did better than placebo on a tinnitus handicap questionnaire (THI) in one 3-month trial in recent-onset tinnitus, by about 7.7 points on average — a difference between group averages. The trial had manufacturer involvement, and no independent repeat was found in our search.
facts: Because it contains many ingredients, the result can’t show which ingredient, if any, helped.
The result says nothing about other products. AUDISTIM, a different formulation, has its own card.

T.name: AUDISTIM
T.alt: AUDISTIM Day/Night
T.desc: A multi-ingredient supplement (containing ginkgo, B vitamins, melatonin and other ingredients) that has been tested against placebo.
human: 1 placebo-controlled trial
120 randomized · 114 analysed
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial

gl.text: Applies to dietary supplements as a group — AUDISTIM is not named in any guideline we checked. AAO-HNSF (2014) recommends against “Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, or other dietary supplements”; European (2019) “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; German (2021) food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.” None of these guidelines assessed this trial.

T.com: The paper states the trial was funded by the manufacturer and run by a contract research centre whose staff are 3 of the 6 authors; separately, the manufacturer’s 2023 promotional sheet lists the other 3 authors as its scientific committee, which the paper’s conflict-of-interest statement does not mention.
T.tells: AUDISTIM Day/Night did better than placebo on a tinnitus handicap questionnaire (THI) in one 3-month trial in chronic tinnitus, by about 7 points on average — a difference between group averages, and the plausible range includes small effects. The trial had manufacturer involvement, and no independent repeat was found in our search.
facts: Because it contains many ingredients, the result can’t show which ingredient, if any, helped.
The result says nothing about other products. Other AUDISTIM products (Jour, RENFORT+) were not tested; MemoVigor 2, a different formulation, has its own card.

T.name: Stomin A
T.alt: Stomin A (ストミンA配合錠), nicotinamide + papaverine
T.desc: A prescription combination tablet in Japan (nicotinamide + papaverine) whose only licensed use is tinnitus.
human: 1 trial · 110 people
compared with plain nicotinamide, not placebo
T.best: Double-blind trial against another medicine
T.qual: Compared with another medicine (plain nicotinamide), not placebo; the difference was not significant at the 5% level in the Japanese guideline’s assessment or our recalculation

gl.text: Japan (2019), in a question that explicitly includes Kampo: drug therapy aimed at eliminating or improving the tinnitus itself “has no evidence and is not appropriate” (weak recommendation, grade 2C). Stomin A is not named in that question; the guideline’s text says its one trial was not significant at the 5% level. No other guideline names Kampo or Stomin A.

T.tells: Stomin A’s one trial compared it with plain nicotinamide for 2 weeks; its package insert calls the result significant, while Japan’s guideline and our recalculation do not. It has never been compared with placebo.
facts: Japanese Kampo herbal formulas are a different kind of treatment and have their own card.

T.name: Japanese Kampo
T.alt: Kampo herbal formulas; Goshajinkigan (牛車腎気丸), Chotosan (釣藤散), Hangekobokuto (半夏厚朴湯), Saireito (柴苓湯), Yokukansan, Tokishakuyakusan and others
T.desc: Traditional Japanese herbal formulas (Kampo) used for tinnitus. About 10 different formulas have been studied, and a result for one formula does not apply to another.
human: About 10 formulas · 1 placebo-controlled trial (76 people) + small studies
4 controlled studies in all (about 400 people) · at least 14 uncontrolled series or reviews
T.best: One double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (hangekobokuto)
T.qual: Differs by formula: hangekobokuto showed no benefit over placebo in 1 trial; other formulas have only small studies

gl.text: Japan (2019), in a question that explicitly includes Kampo: drug therapy aimed at eliminating or improving the tinnitus itself “has no evidence and is not appropriate” (weak recommendation, grade 2C). Its narrative says the effect of Kampo on tinnitus “is not clear,” but its herbal-medicine review covered only ginkgo and bee larvae, not the Kampo trials. No other guideline names Kampo.

T.tells: The only placebo-controlled Kampo trial (hangekobokuto, 12 weeks) found no difference from placebo. Other formulas have only small studies that lacked placebo, adequate randomization or blinding. A result for one formula does not apply to another.
facts: A result for one Kampo formula does not apply to another.
The new Goshajinkigan trial has no comparison group, so it cannot show whether the formula works.
Stomin A, a Japanese prescription medicine, has its own card.

T.name: Ear acupressure seeds & magnets
T.alt: Auricular acupressure, ear seeds, Vaccaria seeds, 耳穴压豆, 耳穴贴压, magnetic ear pellets, magnetic ear clips
T.desc: Seeds, beads or magnets taped to points on the outer ear — sold online and used in Chinese nursing care.
human: Dozens of Chinese trials · at least 21 randomized add-on trials of seeds alone (about 1,900 people)
none compared ear seeds with a sham
T.best: Randomized add-on trials without sham or blinding
T.tells: Dozens of Chinese trials report benefit when ear seeds are added to other care, but none compared them with a sham version, and almost none were blinded. A sham-controlled trial is underway in Taiwan, but it tests ear acupressure together with ear nerve stimulation.

parts.ml: Tested in people — no sham comparison
parts.e: At least 21 randomized add-on trials of seeds alone (about 1,900 people) and many more combined with other treatments; all unblinded and without a sham.

parts.ml: Pellets only, combined with other treatments
parts.e: Magnetic pellets: 3 small Chinese studies, always combined with other treatments. Consumer magnetic ear clips: no studies found in our search.

facts: Needle acupuncture has its own page.
src: Chen S. Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, 2019
Chen Q, et al. Noise Health 2025
Sham-controlled trial of ear nerve stimulation plus magnetic ear beads

T.name: Chinese herbal medicine
T.alt: 耳聋左慈丸, 通窍活血汤 and other formulas
T.desc: Traditional Chinese herbal formulas prescribed for tinnitus.
human: Dozens of studies · thousands of people
T.best: Mostly trials without placebo; 1 published placebo-controlled trial (hearing-loss population)
T.nop: A placebo-controlled trial of an herbal sleep formula in people with insomnia and tinnitus (Taiwan, 108 people; NCT05212298) was completed in January 2026; no public results found in our search.

gl.text: The European (2019) guideline gives a “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies and names traditional Chinese/Korean herbal medicine among them; the German (2021) guideline says food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus” (strong recommendation) and names it among therapies without evidence of efficacy.

T.tells: Many Chinese trials report high “effective rates,” but most added herbs to other treatments without a placebo. The one published placebo-controlled trial, in people with hearing loss, reported a positive composite result; no independent repeat was found in our search.
facts: A placebo-controlled trial in Taiwan (insomnia and tinnitus, 108 people) was completed in January 2026; no public results found in our search.
Chinese medical databases could only be partly searched.
src: Placebo-controlled trial (insomnia and tinnitus), no public results found

T.name: Stellate ganglion block
T.alt: SGB, 星状神经节阻滞
T.desc: An anaesthetic injection into a nerve cluster in the neck, widely offered for tinnitus in China.
human: 11 randomized trials and others · about 1,300 people
T.best: Trials without a sham procedure (none found in our search)
T.tells: Eleven randomized trials in a 2026 meta-analysis report better “effective rates,” but none of them used a sham procedure, and the average difference in questionnaire scores between groups was small (about 6 points).
facts: Rare but serious complications have been reported.
In one trial, the stellate ganglion block group had more side effects than the comparison group.

T.name: Acamprosate
T.alt: Acamprosate; glutamate-modulating medicine
T.desc: A medicine licensed for alcohol dependence that acts on the brain chemical glutamate — sometimes prescribed off-label for tinnitus.
human: 3 placebo-controlled trials · 110 analysed
plus 1 open trial (60); the largest trial (154 enrolled) has no published results
T.best: Small placebo-controlled trials
T.qual: Small positive trials, not confirmed
T.tells: Small placebo-controlled trials of acamprosate were positive, but the largest trial has no published results.

gl.text: The German (2021) guideline names acamprosate in its supporting text (“no evaluated and reproducible therapeutic success”) under its strong recommendation that drugs for chronic tinnitus are “to be avoided.” The European (2019) guideline makes a weak recommendation against drugs for tinnitus in general, without naming this drug. The Japanese (2019) guideline’s evidence text is favourable to this drug class but still advises against drug treatment aimed at the tinnitus itself.

T.nop: Acamprosate trial (NCT00596531, 154 enrolled): completed November 2013; no results posted and no publication found in our search.

T.name: Memantine
T.alt: Memantine; glutamate-modulating medicine
T.desc: A medicine licensed for Alzheimer’s disease that blocks NMDA glutamate channels — sometimes prescribed off-label for tinnitus.
human: 2 trials · about 130 people
plus 1 trial without published results
T.best: Placebo-controlled crossover trial (double-blind)
T.qual: No benefit in the better of 2 small trials
T.tells: The better-designed memantine trial found no benefit. A 2025 trial reporting a benefit used alternating allocation and a co-treatment.

gl.text: The German (2021) guideline names memantine in its supporting text (“no evaluated and reproducible therapeutic success”) under its strong recommendation that drugs for chronic tinnitus are “to be avoided.” The European (2019) guideline makes a weak recommendation against drugs for tinnitus in general, without naming this drug. The Japanese (2019) guideline’s evidence text is favourable to this drug class but still advises against drug treatment aimed at the tinnitus itself.

T.name: Caroverine
T.alt: Caroverine, Spasmium (Austria); glutamate-modulating medicine
T.desc: A muscle-relaxing drug also described as a glutamate-receptor blocker — sold in some countries for tinnitus.
human: At least 14 reports · about 900 people
including comparison groups; plus 1 registered trial without public results
T.best: Randomized placebo-controlled single-infusion trial
T.qual: Mixed: short-term responses after an infusion in some trials; no effect or a fading effect in others
T.tells: Caroverine results are mixed: short-term responses after an infusion in some trials, no effect or a fading effect in others.

gl.text: The German (2021) guideline names caroverine in its supporting text (“no evaluated and reproducible therapeutic success”) under its strong recommendation that drugs for chronic tinnitus are “to be avoided.” The European (2019) guideline makes a weak recommendation against drugs for tinnitus in general, without naming this drug. The Japanese (2019) guideline’s evidence text is favourable to this drug class but still advises against drug treatment aimed at the tinnitus itself.

T.com: The senior author of the 1997 Austrian trial is a co-inventor on a US patent assigned to the manufacturer (Phafag AG) whose claims include tinnitus; Phafag sponsored the suspended Austrian trial; an Indian manufacturer (Entod) supplied the drug for a 2024 study.

T.name: TENS & skin electrical stimulation
T.alt: TENS earpieces, ear-clip TENS, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, cranial electrotherapy (CES, e.g. Alpha-Stim), ear-point microcurrent, RST-Sanexas
T.desc: Home devices that deliver mild electrical stimulation through the skin of the ear, head, neck or jaw.
human: TENS: about 15 controlled trials over 40 years
Cranial electrotherapy: no tinnitus trial found
T.best: Controlled trials of TENS (the device type) — conflicting
T.qual: TENS trials conflict: modest questionnaire changes, no loudness change, very low certainty. No tinnitus trial of cranial electrotherapy was found
T.tells: TENS trials conflict: newer small trials report modest questionnaire changes but no loudness change, and older trials of a wearable home device were negative. No tinnitus trial of cranial electrotherapy was found, and most products sold have not been studied themselves.

gl.text: German (2021): “Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) should not be practiced for chronic tinnitus” (recommendation grade; evidence level 2a). This statement is about TENS only — no guideline position was found for cranial electrotherapy.

T.name: Electromagnetic, radiofrequency & magnet devices
T.alt: Electromagnetic headphones, pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF), Cleanhearing Sono, ACUFREE, Tinniless, radiofrequency stimulation, ear-canal magnets, Magnesphere
T.desc: Home devices that deliver electromagnetic, radiofrequency or magnetic stimulation — for example headphones, ear-canal magnets or a magnetic chair.
human: 3 controlled trials (1991–2004) · conflicting
Most individual products: no study found in our search
T.best: Controlled trials of the device types — conflicting
T.qual: Most products sold have no study of their own found in our search
T.tells: The devices on this card use different technologies, and their evidence does not transfer. Electromagnetic device trials conflict: one 1-week trial was positive, while placebo trials of a pulsed high-frequency device and of ear-canal magnets were negative. Most products sold have not been studied themselves.

T.name: Vitamin B12
T.alt: Methylcobalamin, mecobalamin, 甲钴胺
T.desc: B12 tablets or injections, including methylcobalamin widely used in China and Japan, promoted for “nerve repair.”
human: About 10 studies · about 1,090 people
2 placebo-controlled trials (180 people)
T.best: Placebo-controlled trials (140 and 40 people)
T.tells: In the two placebo-controlled trials, B12 did not do better than placebo for tinnitus overall. A possible benefit was seen only within a small group of people with low B12 levels, without a direct comparison against placebo. Correcting a B12 deficiency is a separate medical question.

a: A possible benefit in a small deficient subgroup (10 people), without a placebo comparison — very low certainty.
b: Question 2: B12 for tinnitus in general
The largest placebo-controlled trial (140 people) found no difference from placebo.

T.qual: For tinnitus in general — 2 small placebo-controlled trials. The deficiency question is separate.

gl.text: The Korean (2026) guideline strongly recommends against routine vitamin supplementation for tinnitus symptom improvement (Grade D†), while noting supplementation may be considered to correct a confirmed deficiency. The European (2019) and German (2021) guidelines list vitamins among supplements without evidence of efficacy, within their recommendations against supplements. Guidelines are not unanimous: the Japanese (2019) guideline says B12 may be worth considering for B12-deficient patients but the evidence is too limited to conclude, and a 2016 Russian guideline — archived by the Russian Ministry of Health in 2021 — recommended a B-vitamin complex at its lowest grade.

T.name: Cutting out caffeine
T.alt: Caffeine withdrawal, decaf, cutting down on coffee or tea
T.desc: Avoiding coffee and other caffeine — a very common piece of tinnitus advice.
human: 1 double-blind withdrawal trial · 66 people
plus 1 single-dose trial (80) and 1 uncontrolled study (26)
T.best: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (described as pseudo-randomized)
T.qual: Based on 1 small double-blind withdrawal trial — it rules out a large average benefit over about 2 weeks, not a benefit for every person
T.tells: In a 30-day double-blind crossover trial, Tinnitus Questionnaire scores were essentially the same on caffeinated and decaffeinated days, and people had caffeine-withdrawal symptoms. A separate trial found that a single caffeine dose did not change tinnitus either.
facts: The German tinnitus guideline (2021) says reducing caffeine has neither a positive nor a negative effect.
A second trial asked a different question (a single caffeine dose) and also found no effect on tinnitus.

T.name: Homeopathic tinnitus products
T.alt: Homeopathic drops and tablets sold for “ringing in the ears”
T.desc: Homeopathic remedies sold over the counter for tinnitus.
human: 3 studies · about 125 people
only 28 in a placebo-controlled trial
T.best: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial (28 people)
T.qual: Based on 1 small placebo-controlled trial

gl.text: The European (2019) guideline gives a “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; homeopathy is named in the supporting text of that section, among therapies for which evidence of efficacy “does not exist.” The German (2021) guideline says food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus” (strong recommendation) and names homeopathy in its supporting text. No other guideline we checked takes a position on homeopathy.

T.tells: In the only placebo-controlled trial (28 people, 1998), a homeopathic remedy did no better than placebo. Apart from one small uncontrolled study of Clear Tinnitus supported by its maker, no study of products sold today was found in our search.

T.name: Magnesium (supplements)
T.alt: Magnesium tablets and capsules
T.desc: Magnesium tablets and capsules sold for tinnitus relief and for protecting hearing from loud noise.
human: 2 studies · about 64 people
T.best: Placebo-controlled trial

gl.text: Applies to dietary supplements as a group — magnesium is not named individually. AAO-HNSF (2014) recommends against “… other dietary supplements”; European (2019) “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; German (2021) food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.”

T.reg: Mayo Clinic placebo-controlled trial (NCT01273883): results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov; no journal publication found in our search.
T.nop: ACEMg open-label study (NCT06477354): completed December 2025; no public results found in our search.
T.qual: Based on 1 small placebo-controlled trial
T.tells: In the only placebo-controlled trial, people rated their tinnitus about the same after magnesium as after placebo. The trial was small and short, and we found its results only in a trial registry.

T.alt: Ozone “autohaemotherapy,” oxygen-ozone therapy, ozonated saline, rectal ozone, ozone injections or ear insufflation
T.desc: Ozone gas given through blood treatment, injection or into the ear, offered by some clinics.

plus about 5 uncontrolled reports; hearing-loss and animal studies kept separate
T.best: Controlled trial with an untreated comparison group (reported as randomized)
T.qual: Based on 1 small, unblinded controlled trial; a second, known only from a secondary summary, also found no difference
T.tells: In a controlled trial, ozone blood treatment did no better than no treatment on loudness or handicap scores over 6 months. A second small placebo-controlled trial, known only from a secondary summary, also found no difference. Serious harms, including gas embolism, have been reported with ozone blood treatments.
facts: The other studies had no comparison group.

T.name: Threshold sound conditioning (TSC)
T.alt: REVE134 · Tinnitogram Signal Generator · “precision sound therapy” (Frequency Health, formerly AudioCardio)
T.desc: A sound-based approach in which a person listens, for short daily sessions, to very quiet sound in chosen frequency bands, set at or near their own hearing threshold. Its inventors propose that this can activate plasticity in the hearing pathway. Two of the software programs used to deliver threshold-level sound have FDA clearance as tinnitus sound generators (“maskers”); clearance of that kind is not evidence that the method treats tinnitus.
human: No published human tinnitus study of TSC identified in our search (28 Sep 2026)
1 small randomized study in hearing loss (39 analysed): hearing thresholds only, no tinnitus measure
T.best: One small randomized study in hearing loss, by the method’s inventors (no tinnitus measure)
T.nop: Two earlier developer-run studies of hearing thresholds (NCT01184248, NCT01434446) are listed as completed; no results were posted and no publication was found in our search.
T.qual: Its only randomized trial was in hearing loss; tinnitus was not measured
T.tells: No published human tinnitus study of TSC, REVE134, or Tinnitogram was identified in our search (28 September 2026). Its one randomized trial, run by the method’s inventors, tested hearing thresholds in people with hearing loss (39 analysed, 2–3 weeks) and did not measure tinnitus. Two software programs that deliver threshold-level sound are FDA-cleared as tinnitus sound generators on the basis of equivalence to earlier devices, not tinnitus trial data.
facts: The two FDA clearances (2015, 2023) are for tinnitus sound generators giving “temporary relief.” They do not establish that TSC improves tinnitus or produces durable benefit. Neither FDA summary reports a clinical trial, and no FDA record identified in our search uses the term “Threshold Sound Conditioning.”

The hearing trial’s conflict-of-interest statement originally read “No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.” A 2021 erratum states that the authors lead the companies involved and that one of them holds intellectual-property ownership of the method.

In our search, the tinnitus-improvement percentages used in the protocol’s marketing (for example “84% of tinnitus patients”) could not be traced to a peer-reviewed publication or trial-registry record.
T.com: Documented in the published record: the 2020 trial lists one affiliation, Sound Vaccine, Inc. (Seoul), and originally stated no conflict of interest. A 2021 erratum corrected this: Sangyeop Kwak is the founder/CEO of Earlogic Korea, Inc. and Chief Science Officer of Sound Vaccine, Inc., and “holds intellectual property ownership over the treatment method described in this study, Threshold Sound Conditioning”; Eunyee Kwak is CEO of Sound Vaccine, Inc. Two registered hearing-threshold studies were sponsored by Earlogic Korea, Inc. A 2026 paper by authors from Sound Vaccine and AudioCardio, Inc. says they are “co-inventors on the TSC-related US patents and applications.” US 11,070,924 B2 (inventors Daehee Lee, Sangyeop Kwak, Sungshin Jang) is listed on Google Patents as assigned to Goldenear Company, Inc., the applicant for the Tinnitogram FDA clearance (K221168). The REVE134 clearance (K151719) was filed by KW Ear Lab, Inc.; its ownership, and any link to the TSC developers, is not stated in the FDA record or in the papers identified in our search. The company’s and a clinic’s web pages describe REVE134 and Tinnitogram as used together in one protocol.

SAFE.peptides: Regulatory statements (US FDA): FDA says it lacks sufficient information to know whether BPC-157 or Semax “would cause harm” when given to people, and its staff reviews (May 2026) recommended against allowing pharmacies to compound them. Anti-doping (WADA 2026 list): BPC-157 is named as prohibited; ARA-290 belongs to a prohibited class our interpretation; Semax and Selank are not named.
SAFE.upper-cervical: Observational association: studies have reported an association between neck manipulation and cervical artery dissection (a tear in a neck artery, which can lead to stroke). An association has been reported; causality has not been established (American Heart Association / American Stroke Association scientific statement, 2014).
SAFE.botox: Regulatory warning (verified on current US FDA labels): all botulinum toxin products carry a boxed warning that effects “may spread from the area of injection”; “Swallowing and breathing difficulties can be life threatening and there have been reports of death.” This class-wide warning covers all uses and is not specific to tinnitus.
SAFE.sgb: Rare but serious complications of stellate ganglion block have been reported (review of complications). In one included trial, the block group reported more side effects than the comparison group.
SAFE.ozone: Regulatory statement (US federal regulation, 21 CFR 801.415): ozone is “a toxic gas with no known useful medical application.” Case reports describe gas embolism (including a death) and a hepatitis C outbreak linked to ozone blood treatments.
SAFE.vinpocetine: Regulatory warning (US FDA, June 2019): vinpocetine may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development; the FDA advises women who are or could become pregnant not to take it. This warning concerns vinpocetine, not piracetam.
SAFE.prp-injections: Injections through the eardrum can cause pain and dizziness (trial reports); one PRP series reported temporary tinnitus as a side effect.
SAFE.stemcell-exosome: Regulatory statements (US FDA): there are no FDA-approved exosome products (2019 notice after serious adverse events in patients treated with unapproved products marketed as containing exosomes). FDA also warns that unapproved stem-cell and other regenerative products have caused serious harms such as blindness, tumours and infections — reported at other body sites. Any injection through the eardrum can cause pain and dizziness (trial reports).
SAFE.ketamine: Randomized-trial adverse events: in one depression trial, short-lived tinnitus followed ketamine injections in about 1 in 4 people vs about 1 in 17 on a comparison drug. Regulatory warning (US FDA label, September 2026): esketamine (Spravato) carries a boxed warning for sedation, dissociation, respiratory depression, abuse and misuse, and suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and is available only through a restricted program. The warning is not about tinnitus.
SAFE.psychedelics: Case report: tinnitus that began after DMT and worsened after psilocybin microdoses. Observational: a US survey linked longer hallucinogen use with tinnitus (an association, not proof of cause). Randomized-trial adverse events: DMT trials report occasional tinnitus.
SAFE.kv7: Regulatory actions: flupirtine medicines were withdrawn in the EU in 2018 because of the risk of serious liver injury (EMA/CMDh, March 2018). Retigabine carried a US boxed warning (2013) and an EU restriction (2013) for retinal and skin pigmentation; its maker stopped selling it worldwide in 2017, stating the reason was very limited use, not safety or effectiveness, and the EU authorisation was withdrawn at the company’s request in 2018.
SAFE.rf-nerve-blocks: Documented procedural risk (review of published cases): serious complications, including rare deaths and brain or spinal cord infarctions, have been reported after steroid injections near nerve roots in the neck (cervical transforaminal injections). This applies to that procedure family, not to every procedure grouped on this card. The tinnitus series of cervical nerve-root infiltration injected at the same site — the openings where nerve roots leave the spine, under X-ray guidance — using dexamethasone, a non-particulate steroid (the papers do not use the word “transforaminal”).
SAFE.stomin-a: Regulatory label (Japan, Stomin A): caution in glaucoma and heart-block; side effects include raised blood pressure, palpitations, dizziness and allergic liver injury (frequency unknown).
SAFE.kampo: Regulatory label warnings (Japan): several Kampo formulas studied for tinnitus list serious side effects — for example interstitial pneumonia (Goshajinkigan, Saireito, Yokukansan) and low potassium with licorice-containing formulas. Two case reports describe lung injury in people taking Kampo (Saireito, Kamikihito) for tinnitus. Warnings are formula-specific; the hangekobokuto label lists no serious side effects.

molecular-hydrogen.claimed: Hydrogen-water bottles and home hydrogen inhalers are sold with tinnitus or “ear health” claims. Sellers usually point to hydrogen’s antioxidant effect. Some cite animal or hearing-loss studies; at least one seller’s tinnitus claim cites no studies at all.

studied.title: People with tinnitus
studied.text: 1 study · 40 people · recent-onset tinnitus · inhaled hydrogen added to a standard medication for 10 days.

studied.title: People with hearing loss
studied.text: 3 studies · 85 people · sudden or radiation-related hearing loss, inhaled hydrogen. These studies measured hearing only; none of the three measured tinnitus.

studied.title: Animals
studied.text: About 20 studies. Hydrogen given before or shortly after noise or drug injury protected the inner ear (prevention or rescue at the time of injury). No animal study measuring tinnitus-like behaviour was found in our search.

studied.title: Laboratory
studied.text: Cell and tissue studies (for example, hair cells exposed to free radicals) showed reduced oxidative damage. This supports biological plausibility for ear protection, not tinnitus treatment.

found.plain: People who breathed in hydrogen alongside the standard medication reported more improvement than people who received the medication alone — on the tinnitus handicap questionnaire and on loudness measures.
numbers: 🧠 85% of the hydrogen group vs 55% of the medication-only group met the study’s THI-based definition of “effective” (reported as statistically significant).
🔉 Loudness ratings and loudness matching decreased more in the hydrogen group (reported as statistically significant; individual values were not available to us).
The researchers concluded hydrogen inhalation “may” improve acute primary tinnitus and needs further clinical verification.

limits: No placebo (sham) inhalation was used, and the published summary does not describe blinding. People may therefore have known which group they were in, which matters because the key tinnitus outcomes were subjective or depended on participants’ responses. our interpretation
Recent-onset tinnitus often improves on its own; both groups improved. Only the difference between the groups is informative.
Small and short: 40 people, 10 days of treatment, no follow-up reported.
The headline result is a category (“effective rate”) based on THI change, rather than an average change with its spread.

Based on the group counts in the device maker’s summary (17 of 20 vs 11 of 20), our recalculation with Fisher’s exact test — often preferred for groups this small — gives p ≈ 0.08, which is not statistically significant. We are not stating which test the authors used. our calculation
Evidence for long-standing (chronic) tinnitus has not been established.
We could not read the full paper, so dropouts, adverse events and conflicts of interest could not be checked.
molecular-hydrogen.repl: No other study of hydrogen in people with tinnitus was found in our search, including in the Chinese, Japanese and English sources we could reach.
molecular-hydrogen.safety:
• Documented in hearing-loss studies: no hydrogen-related adverse events were reported in a 65-person randomized trial, and no serious adverse events in a 17-person uncontrolled study.
  • Animal studies: no adverse effects reported at the inhaled concentrations used (0.5–4%).
  • Tinnitus study: adverse reactions were planned to be recorded; the results were not available to us.
  • Long-term use: not studied.
  • Flammability: hydrogen gas forms flammable, explosive mixtures with air from about 4% by volume (International Chemical Safety Card, ILO/WHO, 2014) — relevant to home inhalation devices.
molecular-hydrogen.guide: No tinnitus guideline statement about hydrogen was found. The European (2019) and German (2021) guideline texts we checked do not mention hydrogen therapy. Other guidelines were not specifically checked for this entry.
molecular-hydrogen.com:
• Tinnitus study: conflicts of interest could not be checked (full text not read). The study is promoted on a hydrogen-device maker’s website; no relationship between the authors and the company was documented, and none is assumed.
  • Hearing-loss trial (not tinnitus): one author of the Japanese randomized trial was employed by MiZ Company Limited, declared in that paper. MiZ’s hydrogen-generating device is named in another published study.
molecular-hydrogen.underway: No registered clinical trial of hydrogen for tinnitus was found in our search.
molecular-hydrogen.why: One small study, in recent-onset tinnitus only, without a placebo, and not repeated. It used inhaled gas, while the products sold are mainly drinking water. Nothing is established for long-standing tinnitus. Animal “ear protection” results are about preventing damage at the moment of injury — a different question from treating tinnitus someone already has.

magnesium.repl: Both human tinnitus studies come from the same Mayo Clinic group. The Iranian placebo-controlled trial would be independent, but no results were found in our search.
magnesium.safety:
• Documented in the trial: 3 people withdrew because of side effects during the first period; 7 of 38 reported other side effects while taking magnesium.
  • General: high-dose magnesium supplements often cause diarrhoea, and the risk of too much magnesium in the blood is higher in people with reduced kidney function (US National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements, 2026).
magnesium.guide: No guideline names magnesium specifically. Broad statements about dietary supplements as a group apply: the AAO-HNSF (2014) guideline recommends against “Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, or other dietary supplements” for persistent, bothersome tinnitus; the European (2019) guideline gives a “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; and the German (2021) guideline says food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus.” Magnesium tablets fall into this supplement group, but none of these guidelines evaluates magnesium on its own.
magnesium.com:
• Mayo Clinic studies: no conflicts of interest documented in the research reviewed.
  • ACEMg open-label study: sponsored by the manufacturer, Keep Hearing, Inc. (registry).
magnesium.underway: No active trial of magnesium for tinnitus was found in our search. The Iranian placebo-controlled trial has finished recruiting but has no results; the manufacturer-run study has no comparison group, so it cannot show whether magnesium works.
magnesium.why: The only placebo-controlled trial showed essentially the same change with magnesium and placebo, but it was small and short, and we found no journal publication of it. A second placebo-controlled trial in Iran has finished recruiting; its results could change this entry.
magnesium.cov: PubMed, Europe PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Iranian trial registry were searched. The key placebo-controlled trial was found through the ClinicalTrials.gov results database, not PubMed.

sgb.claimed: Hospital pages, mainly in China, describe stellate ganglion block as improving blood flow to the inner ear and brain and restoring “autonomic balance.” One hospital news page reports a patient’s tinnitus “disappearing” with an “immediate effect” after one course of blocks — a single-patient anecdote.

studied.title: People with tinnitus
studied.text: At least 17 reports, about 1,300 people in total — including 11 randomized trials (915 people) pooled in a 2026 meta-analysis, plus retrospective and older uncontrolled series.

studied.title: Circulation measurements
studied.text: Blood-flow velocities in neck and brain arteries were pooled in the meta-analysis. A change in blood flow is not evidence that tinnitus improved.

studied.title: Animals
studied.text: No animal study measuring tinnitus-like behaviour after stellate ganglion block was found in our search.

sgb.special:
Many studies ≠ strong controlled evidence
11 randomized trials · 915 people

All added the block to medicines; people knew whether they received it. None used a sham procedure.

Why a sham matters here

A neck injection is a vivid, invasive experience, and tinnitus is rated by how people feel. Without a look-alike “sham” injection, hope, attention and the added medicines can’t be separated from the effect of the block itself. Adding more unblinded trials doesn’t solve that problem.

The 11 trials also used four different definitions of “effective,” yet their results were statistically almost identical (I² = 0%) — a pattern that can suggest reporting bias. our interpretation

found.plain: The trials report that more people improved when the block was added to medicines. But on the tinnitus questionnaire (THI), the average extra improvement was small.
numbers: Composite “effective rate” (11 trials, 915 people): odds ratio 4.53 in favour of adding the block. This combines subjective improvement categories defined in four different ways.

🧠 THI (5 trials, 289 people): average difference between groups −5.7 points. A change of about 7 THI points is a threshold for change noticed by an individual patient (Zeman et al. 2011; other studies suggest higher values). It is not a threshold for a difference between group averages, so the two should not be compared directly.
The meta-analysis authors rated certainty “moderate to low.” Their funnel plot looked asymmetric (a possible sign of missing small negative studies; statistical test p = 0.16).
A non-randomized Korean comparison (1998) found no statistically significant difference between medicines, the block, and both combined (improvement 28%, 33% and 42%).

limits: No sham procedure in any randomized trial found — expectations and the added medicines can’t be separated from the block.
Open-label (unblinded) and add-on designs.
Main outcome is a composite “effective rate,” defined four different ways.
The average THI difference between groups was small (−5.7 points).
Short follow-up: most trials reported results only at the end of treatment.
Possible reporting bias (asymmetric funnel plot; identical results across different definitions).
Some trials are not independent of each other (same hospital, overlapping authors).
One retrospective series found that people with the highest starting scores improved most — consistent with natural “regression to the mean.” our interpretation
sgb.repl: The trials come from several nominally different Chinese centres, so there is replication on paper. However, two known groups of reports share a hospital or first author, all trials share the same unblinded add-on design, and no controlled trial outside China was found. Replication of an unblinded design does not remove its bias. our interpretation
sgb.safety:
• Documented serious complications (systematic review of stellate ganglion block, 1990–2018): 260 adverse-event cases in 67 articles, including one death from bleeding that blocked the airway and one case of quadriplegia from a spinal abscess. These are rare, but they are documented.
  • In tinnitus trials: reported side effects included nausea, dizziness, hoarseness, throat discomfort and coughing. In one trial (92 people), side effects were statistically more frequent in the block group.
  • Tinnitus worsening: in the 1998 Korean comparison, tinnitus worsened in 5.2% of treated ears (a non-randomized observation).
sgb.guide: No guideline position was found. Stellate ganglion block is not mentioned in the Japanese (2019), German (2021), European (2019) or NICE (2020) tinnitus guidelines, or in the pages of the 2024 Chinese integrated-medicine consensus we could access. Why many studies don’t add up to strong evidence here
Different formulas

Trials test many different herbal combinations, chosen by traditional pattern diagnosis. A result for one formula is not evidence for another.

Different comparisons

coq10.special:
Registry record compared with the published paper

The trial was registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20120215009014N339). The paper does not cite this registration; we matched the two by investigators, doses, duration, size and population. our matching

  • Timing of the assessment — resolved. The English version of the registry record says outcomes were measured “6 months later.” The original Persian version of the same record says 6 weeks, matching the 6-week treatment and the paper. The English wording is most likely a translation error in the registry our interpretation; it is not a change of time point between registry and paper.
  • Registered after recruitment began. The registry itself classes the record as “registered while recruiting”: registered 7 February 2020, about four and a half months after the expected start of recruitment (23 September 2019). Actual recruitment dates were never entered, and the record has not been updated.
  • Outcomes. The registry lists three main (primary) outcomes: tinnitus handicap (THI), sleep, and quality of life. The paper found no significant difference for quality of life and does not name a primary outcome. Tinnitus loudness, reported in the paper as a positive result, is not a registered outcome.
  • Other differences. Blinding (registry: triple-blind; paper: double-blind), randomization method (registry: drawing lots; paper: random number table) and entry criteria (registry: age 50–90 and tinnitus for over a year; paper: tinnitus for at least six months, no age limit stated). The paper does not explain these differences.

Registry differences do not by themselves mean a result is wrong. They make it harder to confirm that the reported outcomes were the ones planned. our interpretation

Reading the two headline numbers
“0 of 16”

In a randomized trial of manganese, everyone took Lipo-Flavonoid Plus; one group also took manganese. Of the 16 people who finished the Lipo-Flavonoid-only group, none showed a decrease on the tinnitus questionnaires. b12.special:
Two different questions
Question 1 · Tinnitus in general

Two placebo-controlled trials (180 people). Neither found a clear difference from placebo on tinnitus severity. A 2026 Korean guideline pooled these trials with one other vitamin trial and found an average THI difference between groups of −0.6 points — essentially none.

Question 2 · People with a confirmed B12 deficiency

In one trial (40 people), 10 people with low B12 given B12 injections improved compared with their own starting scores; 7 people with low B12 given saline did not change. The two groups were not compared directly, the subgroup was not described as planned in advance, and the finding has not been repeated independently. Very low certainty.

This page does not give individual medical advice. Whether someone has a B12 deficiency, and how to treat it, is a question for their own doctor.

found.plain: Neither placebo-controlled trial found that B12 reduced tinnitus more than placebo. In the smaller trial, people with low B12 who received injections improved compared with their own starting scores, but they were not directly compared with the people with low B12 who received saline.
numbers: 2024 trial (140 people): THI and severity ratings did not differ from placebo at 1 or 3 months (THI P = 0.13 and 0.09; VAS P = 0.49 and 0.25). The authors concluded B12 had no distinctive effect on tinnitus severity.
2016 trial (40 people): patient-rated improvement in 6 of 20 with B12 vs 4 of 20 with saline — not statistically significant.

Deficient subgroup, B12 injections (10 people): Tinnitus Severity Index 36.5 → 28.3 (within-group P = 0.016). Deficient subgroup, saline (7 people): 32.8 → 32.3. No direct comparison between these groups was reported.
Korean guideline pooled analysis (2026): THI difference −0.6 points; tinnitus severity rating +0.1.

limits: Only two placebo-controlled trials, both small (40 and 140 people).

The possible benefit in deficient people rests on 10 treated people compared with their own starting scores; the subgroup was not described as planned in advance, and randomization was not stratified by B12 level.
The 2016 trial excluded people with anaemia and did not report B12 levels after treatment, so it is unclear whether the deficiency was corrected.
The 2016 trial’s reported statistics are internally inconsistent (the degrees of freedom fit a different test from the one named). our reading
The 2024 trial did not report measuring B12 levels.
Most people studied were in uncontrolled Japanese series from decades ago; without comparison groups, natural improvement — especially in recent-onset tinnitus — cannot be separated from treatment.
A 2026 review misdescribes the 2024 trial as a positive 80-person injection trial; this page follows the original publication. our finding
b12.repl: For tinnitus in general, two placebo-controlled trials by different research teams (India, Iran) both found no clear benefit. For people with a deficiency, the subgroup finding has not been repeated independently: a 2024 study from the same Indian institution compared two forms of B12 without a placebo, and a 2023 Egyptian report with the same design raises integrity questions (see above).
b12.safety:
• In the trials: the 2024 trial reported no noticeable side effects in either group; older Japanese series reported none. The 2016 injection trial did not report adverse events.
  • Guideline review (Korea 2026): no serious adverse events were reported, but all trials were small and short, leaving insufficient long-term safety evidence.
  • Not established in the research reviewed: safety of long-term, high-dose use for tinnitus.
b12.guide:
Guidelines disagree.

Recommend against routine use

Korea (2026): clinicians “should not recommend vitamin supplementation as routine treatment” for tinnitus symptoms — Grade D†, a strong recommendation made despite low-certainty evidence. Its evidence includes both B12 trials. It adds that supplementation may be considered to correct a confirmed deficiency. Europe (2019) and Germany (2021): vitamins are listed among supplements without evidence of efficacy, within recommendations against (Europe) or to omit (Germany) supplements.

Other positions

Japan (2019): B12 may be a treatment possibility for people with tinnitus and B12 deficiency, but the supporting literature is too limited to reach a conclusion; the same guideline advises against drug treatment aimed at eliminating tinnitus itself (grade 2C). Russia (2016, archived in 2021): recommended a B-vitamin complex, including B12, at its lowest grade (C); the Russian Ministry of Health archived this guideline in May 2021 when its validity period expired. NICE (2020): no statement on vitamins.

Guideline wording checked against the guideline texts. No current Russian tinnitus guideline was found.
b12.com: No commercial involvement documented. The 2016 trial was funded by the university’s educational trust, with no conflicts of interest declared; the 2024 trial’s authors declare no conflicts of interest; no funding statement was visible in the parts of the paper we could read. B12 is an ingredient in several combination tinnitus products; those products are not assessed here.
b12.underway: No registered trial of B12 on its own for tinnitus was found in our search. A completed and published placebo-controlled trial of a combination product containing B12 (AUDISTIM, NCT05300594) cannot isolate B12’s effect; it is described on its own card.
b12.why: For tinnitus in general, both placebo-controlled trials found no clear benefit over placebo. For people with a B12 deficiency, the only signal comes from 10 treated people compared with their own starting scores, and it has not been repeated. Correcting a diagnosed deficiency is a medical question in its own right — separate from whether B12 treats tinnitus.

botox.claimed: Some clinics offer botulinum toxin injections into jaw, neck or ear muscles as an off-label treatment for tinnitus. One hearing-care company’s article says Botox may be “little more than a placebo” for some forms of tinnitus but is supported by research for others, citing a migraine observation and case series in muscle-spasm tinnitus. None of the current US FDA labels lists tinnitus as an approved use.

A further placebo-controlled trial (41 people) has finished, with no results found in our search.

studied.text: Retrospective case series and reviews of case reports in spasm of palate or middle-ear muscles, and in hemifacial spasm. Shown separately below; results do not transfer to ordinary tinnitus.
