botox.special:
Two different conditions
Subjective tinnitus — often linked to jaw or neck muscles

The sound only the person hears. This card. Evidence: one small placebo-controlled trial (2005) and a few case reports. A 100-person placebo-controlled trial in people with severe jaw clenching is underway in Norway.

Objective “clicking” tinnitus from muscle spasm

Rhythmic clicking caused by spasms of small muscles in the palate or middle ear. Evidence: retrospective case series without comparison groups — for example, 57 people with middle-ear muscle spasm treated in Korea (2026), and a review of 51 treated people with palatal tremor that its authors rated extremely low evidence. A different condition; not counted in this card’s classification.

botox.repl: No repeat of the 2005 trial has been published. A 41-person placebo-controlled trial at the University of Minnesota finished in December 2025, with no results found in our search, and a 100-person trial is underway in Norway.
botox.safety:
• Regulatory warning (current US FDA labels, checked 24 Sep 2026): every botulinum toxin product carries a boxed warning that the toxin’s effects may spread from the injection site; swallowing and breathing difficulties can be life-threatening, and deaths have been reported. The warning is class-wide — it covers all botulinum toxin products and uses — and is not specific to tinnitus.
  • Label reports: the BOTOX label lists tinnitus and reduced hearing among side effects reported after approval, noting that a causal link cannot be established.
  • In tinnitus studies: side effects in the 2005 trial could not be checked (full text not accessible), and the Minnesota trial has no posted results. Case series in objective tinnitus reported no or only mild complications.
botox.guide: No guideline position was found on botulinum toxin for tinnitus. It is not mentioned in the European (2019), German (2021) or NICE (2020) guidelines. The Japanese (2019) guideline mentions reports of benefit in palatal myoclonus — objective tinnitus only — as narrative, not a graded recommendation. The European guideline makes a weak recommendation against drug treatments for tinnitus in general, and the German guideline says drugs for chronic tinnitus should be avoided; neither names botulinum toxin, and we do not apply these general statements to it. For tinnitus that changes with jaw or neck problems, the German guideline recommends manual therapy and physiotherapy — a different treatment. The AAO-HNSF (2014) full text was not checked for this entry.
botox.com:
• University of Minnesota trial (NCT05650645): a University of Minnesota Medical School news page states that the lead investigator’s research on this treatment is funded by a research grant from Merz Pharma, which makes Xeomin — the product used in the trial. The registry lists no collaborator, so whether the grant funds this specific trial is our inference, not documented. our inference
  • 2005 trial: the paper’s funding and drug-supply statement could not be checked (full text not accessible).
  • TINNITOX (Norway): non-commercial hospital sponsor, funded by the Norwegian association of practising specialists. It uses a marketed BOTOX product (AbbVie); no manufacturer support is recorded.
  • 2026 scoping review: its authors declare affiliations with aesthetic-medicine companies.

Company funding or drug supply does not by itself make a study’s results wrong.
botox.underway: Registry note: the Minnesota record (below) is registered as a parallel-group trial, but its wording (“placebo for the first stage”, “three serial injections”) suggests the placebo group may later have received the toxin; the design should be confirmed when results appear. our interpretation Under US rules, results are expected about 12 months after completion — around December 2026. our reading of the rule
botox.why: The only placebo-controlled trial is small, about 20 years old and not repeated, and its only difference from placebo was on a patient-rated better/same/worse question. Two newer placebo-controlled trials — one finished without published results, one underway in a narrower group with severe jaw clenching — may change this entry.

antinitus.special:
Main measure versus responder result
Main measure — planned

Change in tinnitus annoyance (0–10 rating) after 3 weeks of patches, compared with placebo. The paper calls this “the primary variable,” and the trial size was calculated for it. Result: no difference from placebo.

Responder result — secondary

A “responder” was someone whose annoyance rating fell by at least 2 points at week 7 (4 weeks after stopping). 12 of 41 (29%) with the patch vs 4 of 41 (10%) with placebo; P = 0.049, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons. The trial was not registered, so whether this analysis was planned in advance cannot be checked. Average annoyance and THI at week 7 did not differ.

Regulatory history (Sweden)
  • Sweden’s Medical Products Agency (Läkemedelsverket) — government report: its 2018 market-surveillance follow-up (dated 12 March 2019) records a marketing ban on a patch claimed to relieve tinnitus, after the agency found no scientific basis for the proposed mechanism of action. The report does not name the product and notes that the manufacturer appealed.
  • Manufacturer’s own regulatory announcement (29 October 2018): Sensori stated that it had received the agency’s decision prohibiting Antinitus from being placed on the market, that the agency found the study results could not demonstrate an effect, and that it would appeal. This is what links the agency’s report to Antinitus.
  • Stock exchange: on 4 September 2018 the Nordic Growth Market disciplinary committee fined Sensori SEK 100,000 over press releases claiming significant effects, recording that the trial’s main measure showed no difference from placebo.
  • Court outcome — secondary sources only: the company’s own year-end report (27 February 2019) confirms that it appealed the ban to the administrative court. The Swedish hearing-loss association (HRF) reported in January 2020 that the court in Uppsala rejected the appeal in full and that the company had appealed again, to the administrative court of appeal in Stockholm, so the ban was not yet final. We found no published judgment and no record of the final outcome. The company was later wound up: Sweden’s companies register records a bankruptcy closed in August 2020 and a liquidation completed in October 2021.
  • Where the ban applied: we found no agency or EU document stating the ban’s geographical reach, and no EU-level decision. When it announced its appeal, the company said Antinitus would remain available “for sale outside the EU”; Swedish news reports at the time said the ban covered the whole EU and EEA.

antinitus.repl: No independent published trial. An investigator-led trial in Türkiye (NCT07731230, 91 enrolled) finished in 2021, but it was first registered in July 2026, and no results have been published or posted.
antinitus.safety:
• In the placebo-controlled trial: reversible skin irritation in 24% with the patch vs 17% with placebo (not a significant difference); no serious events reported.
  • Pilot study and user surveys: no safety concerns reported.
  • The Swedish ban was based on the lack of a scientific basis for the claimed mechanism, not on reported harm.
antinitus.guide: No guideline position was found. Antinitus and similar patches are not mentioned in the European (2019), German (2021) or NICE (2020) guidelines. The German guideline’s recommendation against low-level laser therapy concerns an active laser device, and we do not apply it to this passive patch.
antinitus.com:
• Placebo-controlled trial: the Nordic Growth Market stock exchange’s market surveillance describes it as a placebo study that “the Company conducted” (2018 annual report; our translation from Swedish), and the company’s press releases referred to “our study programme.” The paper itself has no funding or conflict-of-interest statement; the authors are listed with ENT clinics.
  • Pilot study: registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01226108) by Akloma Bioscience AB, an industry sponsor, with the arm labelled “antinitus patch”; the published pilot names the device maker as Akloma Tinnitus AB. That the registry record and the paper describe the same study is our inference. our inference
  • Independent trial (NCT07731230): registered as investigator-initiated at Istanbul Medeniyet University, with no industry collaborator listed. Who supplied the active and placebo patches, and how the trial was funded, is not disclosed.

Company involvement does not by itself make a result wrong.
antinitus.underway: No active or recruiting trial was found in our search; the two records below are listed because no results have been posted. Registration timing: NCT07731230 started in June 2018, was completed in February 2021, and was first registered on 23 July 2026. When a trial is registered after its data exist, the registry cannot confirm which outcome was planned as the main one. our interpretation The record also gives two participant numbers (91 enrolled; “eighty participants took part”).
antinitus.why: In the only published placebo-controlled trial, run by the manufacturer, the planned main measure showed no difference from placebo; the one positive result was a secondary analysis. No plausible mechanism has been shown, and Sweden’s medical products agency found no scientific basis for the claimed mechanism. An independent trial finished in 2021 but has not reported results; its results could change this entry.

nac.claimed: NAC is promoted as an antioxidant that “protects hair cells” and reduces tinnitus, especially after noise. Much of the promotion draws on research about preventing noise- or drug-related hearing damage, not on studies of people who already have tinnitus.

studied.title: Treating established tinnitus
studied.text: 2 single-patient reports (2013, 2023). No controlled trial of NAC as a treatment for existing tinnitus was found in our search.

studied.title: Prevention and hearing protection
studied.text: Placebo-controlled and other trials of NAC to protect hearing — during ear surgery, in nightclub-goers, in military recruits, and during cisplatin chemotherapy. Some recorded tinnitus as a secondary result. People did not need to have tinnitus to take part, and these trials test prevention, not treatment.

studied.title: Animals
studied.text: Tinnitus-like behaviour has been tested only with NAC combined with an experimental drug (HPN-07), by one research group with declared commercial interests. No animal tinnitus study of NAC on its own was found.

studied.title: Laboratory
studied.text: Antioxidant effects on inner-ear cells. These support ideas about protection, not tinnitus treatment.

nac.special:
Has NAC actually been tested as a tinnitus treatment?

Not in any controlled trial found in our search. The only studies of NAC in people who already had tinnitus are two single-patient reports:

Case report, 2013

A woman in a depression trial of NAC (2 g a day by mouth) said her tinnitus had “largely disappeared.” Her depression lifted almost completely at the same time, and no tinnitus questionnaire was used.

Case report, 2023

A man with severe tinnitus after ear-nerve tumour surgery had taken NAC (2,500 mg twice a day) for months without significant improvement. Improvement (THI 86 → 40) followed only after an experimental drug (OKN-007) was added.

Trials of NAC to prevent hearing damage are shown separately below. Their results cannot be used as evidence that NAC treats tinnitus someone already has. our interpretation
best: Two single-patient reports — no controlled treatment trial found
Dean 2013, African Journal of Psychiatry — 47-year-old woman in an NAC depression trial; oral NAC 2 g a day; tinnitus described in her own words; depression remitted at the same time

Kesari et al. 2023, International Tinnitus Journal — man with tinnitus after vestibular schwannoma surgery; oral NAC 2,500 mg twice a day since 2020 without significant improvement; improvement after an added IV experimental drug
Report 1: none (patient description). Report 2: 🧠 THI 86 → 40; 🔉 loudness match 90 → 19 dB
Largest controlled study with a tinnitus result (prevention)
Bagger-Sjöbäck et al. 2015, PLoS One — 156 people having ear (stapes) surgery; one IV NAC infusion vs matching placebo, double-blind; tinnitus 0–10 rating was a secondary outcome at 1 year

found.plain: Neither case report gives a usable signal for NAC on its own. In prevention trials that recorded tinnitus, the placebo-controlled results showed no difference.
numbers: Surgery trial (prevention; 139 analysed): tinnitus rating change at 1 year 1.07 with NAC vs 1.24 with placebo — no significant difference. The authors concluded NAC had no effect on hearing, tinnitus or balance.
Nightclub trial (prevention; 31 healthy people, one dose): no significant difference in tinnitus measures — reported in a later review by an author of the trial; the full text was not accessible.
Military trial (prevention; 566 recruits): tinnitus questionnaires were given, but tinnitus results are not in the published abstract; the full text was not accessible.

Cisplatin study (prevention): no new tinnitus in 48 ears injected with NAC vs 20 of 48 ears injected with dexamethasone — no placebo, and each person had one ear of each, which makes it hard to attribute new tinnitus to one ear. our interpretation

limits: No controlled trial of NAC as a treatment for existing tinnitus was found in our search.
Both case reports have major confounders: depression remission in one, an added experimental drug in the other.
The controlled trials test prevention — mostly single doses before noise or surgery, or injections during chemotherapy — in people who did not need to have tinnitus.
Tinnitus was a secondary or unreported outcome in most prevention trials.
A NAC-plus-magnesium prevention trial (Belgium) has had registry status “unknown” since 2013, and no results were found.
nac.repl: Not applicable — there is no positive controlled treatment result to repeat.
nac.safety:
• Regulatory label (UK, oral NAC): tinnitus is listed as an uncommon side effect (between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 100 people); other uncommon effects include stomach upset, headache and allergic reactions. A listed side effect is not proof that NAC causes tinnitus.
  • Regulatory label (US, intravenous NAC): the prescribing information warns of serious, sometimes fatal allergic (anaphylactic) reactions — relevant to the IV form used in some trials, not to oral supplements.
  • Randomized-trial adverse events: in the surgery trial, 4 people given IV NAC had vomiting, flushing or vein irritation (none with placebo); in the military trial, side effects were similar with NAC and placebo (27% vs 27%).
nac.guide: No treatment-specific guideline position found. NAC is not named in the AAO-HNSF (2014), European (2019), German (2021), NICE (2020), Japanese (2019) or Korean (2026) guidelines. Several guidelines recommend against dietary supplements as a group; we have not applied those statements to NAC, because NAC is a prescription medicine in some countries and is outside the legal definition of a dietary supplement in the US. our interpretation
nac.com:
• 2023 case report: a co-author is founder and equity-holder in a company that licensed the experimental drug (OKN-007) to the company that supplied it; another co-author is a vice president of that supplier (declared in the paper). The commercial interest concerns the added drug, not NAC.
  • Surgery trial: publicly funded; the trial registry lists AstraZeneca as a collaborator (role not stated); the paper declares no competing interests.
  • Other: a US company announced in 2003 that it had licensed US Navy NAC hearing-protection technology; no role for it in any published trial was documented.

Company involvement does not by itself make a study’s results wrong.
nac.underway: The only active NAC tinnitus study found is a small single-group study of a combination treatment, which cannot show whether NAC itself helps.
nac.why: NAC has not been tested as a treatment for established tinnitus in any controlled trial found in our search. The two case reports are confounded, and in one of them NAC alone had not helped. The controlled research is about preventing hearing damage, and the placebo-controlled results that recorded tinnitus showed no difference.

All in people with neck problems
upper-cervical.claimed: Upper-cervical chiropractic practices and directories describe neck adjustments as addressing a “root cause” of tinnitus. One practitioner directory cites a 2011 upper-cervical chiropractic study as showing improvement in tinnitus; in that study’s full text, “ringing in the ears” appears only as a possible side effect, and no tinnitus outcome is reported. our reading of the source A 2021 review of 287 French chiropractic websites found tinnitus mentioned on 56 of them.

studied.title: People with tinnitus and neck problems
studied.text: About a dozen reports, about 60 people: one retrospective series of neck manipulation by physicians (47 people with tinnitus) and about 11 single-patient reports by chiropractors or manual-medicine doctors. Every report involved people with neck complaints.

studied.title: Tinnitus in general
studied.text: No study tested neck manipulation in people with tinnitus who were not selected for neck problems.

studied.title: Related but different treatments
studied.text: Physiotherapy for neck- or jaw-related tinnitus (mobilisation, exercise, trigger-point work) has its own page and is not counted here. Osteopathy and combinations with acupuncture are also different treatments.

upper-cervical.special:
Which intervention was actually studied?
Physician neck manipulation (German manual medicine) best evidence
Studies
1 retrospective series (Hülse & Hölzl 2004) and 1 single-patient report
Technique
Manipulation “particularly of the atlanto-occipital joint” (top of the neck), delivered by doctors
Result
Only 10% of 47 people with tinnitus improved
Upper-cervical-specific chiropractic
Studies
Single-patient reports (for example 2000 and 2026), knee-chest and similar techniques
Result
Symptoms reported as improved or resolved in individual patients; no comparison group
General chiropractic spinal manipulation
Studies
About 5 single-patient reports, some combined with acupuncture or exercise; 2 in people with a Ménière’s diagnosis
Result
Individual improvements; co-treatments prevent attributing them to manipulation
Traditional manipulation (Chinese tuina, Korean Chuna)
Studies
1 randomized trial (120 people) of acupuncture plus spinal tuina vs acupuncture alone; 2 Korean case reports with multiple treatments
Result
Higher “curative rate” with the combination; no sham, and the manipulation effect cannot be separated from different acupuncture points

These are different techniques, delivered by different practitioners. The page does not treat them as interchangeable.
best: Hülse M, Hölzl M, 2004 — HNO (University ENT clinic, Mannheim, Germany; in German)
Retrospective long-term follow-up; no comparison group
People with ear, nose and throat symptoms attributed to the neck
Yes — the series selected people with neck-related disorders
Neck manipulation by physicians, particularly of the top joint of the neck (not chiropractic)
Patient-rated improvement (loudness and distress not reported separately in the abstract)
Peer-reviewed; abstract read (full text in German, not accessible)

found.plain: In the only series with more than one patient, most people with neck-related tinnitus did not improve after neck manipulation.
numbers: “Only 10%” of 47 people with tinnitus showed an improvement (retrospective, no comparison group).
Single-patient reports describe tinnitus easing or resolving after chiropractic or manual-medicine care, often together with other treatments.
Acupuncture plus spinal tuina vs acupuncture alone (120 people): “curative rate” 70% vs 45% — a composite effective-rate outcome, without a sham or blinding.

limits: No sham-controlled trial of chiropractic or upper-cervical adjustment for tinnitus was found in our search.
All positive reports are single patients with neck problems; many also received other treatments.
The one larger series used physician manipulation and found only 10% improved.
No study tested tinnitus in general, so results in people with neck problems cannot be applied to everyone with tinnitus.
Chinese databases could not be searched directly, so Chinese-language trials of neck manipulation may have been missed.
upper-cervical.repl: Not applicable — there is no positive controlled result to repeat.
upper-cervical.safety:
• Observational association (serious, rare): studies have reported an association between neck manipulation and cervical artery dissection — a tear in a neck artery, which can lead to stroke. An association has been reported; causality has not been established. The American Heart Association / American Stroke Association scientific statement (2014) says biomechanical evidence is insufficient to establish that manipulation causes dissection, and advises that patients be told about the statistical association.
  • Controlled observational studies: a large case-control study (2008) found similar associations for chiropractor and family-doctor visits, which suggests that people with an early dissection may seek care for neck pain; a 2016 meta-analysis found a small association with very low certainty and no convincing evidence of a causal link.
  • Case reports: individual cases of dissection after manipulation have been published; these show timing, not cause.
  • Common minor reactions (randomized trials and cohorts): temporary soreness or headache; in a cohort of 1,090 upper-cervical chiropractic patients, 31% reported a reaction within 24 hours, mostly mild.
  • Relevant to tinnitus: new pulsing (pulsatile) tinnitus with neck pain can be a sign of artery dissection and is a reason for medical assessment; the AHA/ASA statement lists pulsatile tinnitus among the ways dissection can present our interpretation.
upper-cervical.guide: No treatment-specific guideline position found on chiropractic or upper-cervical adjustment. The German (2021) guideline says manual medical and physiotherapeutic therapy “should be offered” for chronic tinnitus when tinnitus is modulated by neck or jaw problems; its evidence comes from mobilisation, myofascial, osteopathic and exercise studies, and it does not name chiropractic or upper-cervical adjustment. We do not apply it to this card. The European (2019), NICE (2020), Japanese (2019) and Korean (2026) guidelines make no statement on neck manipulation, and no guideline recommends against it.
upper-cervical.com:
• No commercial funding of any tinnitus study was documented.
  • Most single-patient reports were written by practitioners who deliver the treatment (for example, one author’s own chiropractic clinic); this is a professional interest, not a documented financial disclosure.
  • Practitioner directories and clinics promote upper-cervical care for tinnitus; one cites a study that did not measure tinnitus (see “What is claimed?”).
upper-cervical.underway: No active or upcoming trial of chiropractic or upper-cervical adjustment for tinnitus was found in our search. The two finished osteopathy trials below include some neck thrust techniques but do not isolate them.
upper-cervical.why: Only case reports and one uncontrolled series exist, all in people with neck problems, and the series found that only 10% improved. No sham-controlled trial was found, and no study tested people with tinnitus in general.
upper-cervical.cov: PubMed, Europe PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN, the Iranian registry, and Chinese, Korean, Japanese, German and Persian web sources were searched. Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang), several national registries and chiropractic-specific indexes could not be searched directly. How this entry was corrected: our earlier count (about 6 reports, about 50 people) missed 7 single-patient reports, and the best study was delivered by physicians, not chiropractors.

chips: Two different drugs — evidence kept separate
No placebo-controlled tinnitus trial of either found
vinpocetine.claimed: Vinpocetine (Cavinton) is prescribed in Russia, neighbouring countries and Hungary to “improve blood flow” to the brain and inner ear, including for ear noise. Piracetam (Nootropil) is a “nootropic” (brain-function) drug also used in courses for hearing and ear symptoms. Improved cerebral or inner-ear blood flow is a proposed mechanism, not evidence that tinnitus improves.

studied.title: People with tinnitus — vinpocetine
studied.text: 5 studies (Russia, Czech Republic, Germany, Poland, India), several with vinpocetine as one of many groups. No placebo-controlled trial of vinpocetine alone for tinnitus was found.

studied.title: People with tinnitus — piracetam
studied.text: 2 small randomized studies against other medicines (Germany 1995, Greece 2004), both in sudden hearing loss or noise injury, plus a non-randomized Indian study and a case report. No placebo-controlled trial found.

studied.title: Hearing loss
studied.text: Studies of vinpocetine in sudden or long-standing hearing loss (Russia, China, Mexico) report hearing results. They are not counted as tinnitus evidence.

studied.title: Mechanism
studied.text: Vinpocetine: blood-vessel widening and effects on nerve ion channels. Piracetam: effects on cell membranes and blood-cell clumping. Neither is a tinnitus outcome.

vinpocetine.studiedNote: Piracetam is also used for muscle-spasm (myoclonic) tinnitus, a different condition with a different mechanism; that use is not counted here.
vinpocetine.special:
Two drugs, two evidence streams
Vinpocetine (Cavinton) mostly open studies
What it is
A semi-synthetic compound derived from the periwinkle plant; blood-flow drug. Maker of Cavinton: Gedeon Richter (Hungary)
Where used for ear noise
Russia, neighbouring countries, Hungary, China
Studies
Russia 2009 (50 people with chronic hearing loss, open; ear noise reported “reduced”, no numbers) · Czech Republic 2008 (150 people with chronic tinnitus in 7 treatment groups, 54 given vinpocetine; described as both retrospective and randomly divided; no placebo) · Germany 1986 (400 soldiers after acute noise injury; saline control; adding vinpocetine gave no extra benefit) · Poland 1997 (20 people after noise injury; vinpocetine vs nicergoline) · India 2021 (130 people; 5 active groups, one vinpocetine alone; all improved within groups)
Comparator
Mostly other drugs; the only saline comparison was in acute noise injury, as an add-on
Tinnitus endpoint
Rating scales (VAS), modified THI, or “improvement” — rarely a validated questionnaire
Result
Open studies reported improvement; the one saline-controlled programme showed no added benefit
Independent replication
No placebo-controlled study to repeat
Piracetam (Nootropil) 2 small randomized comparisons
What it is
A “nootropic” drug related to the brain chemical GABA. UK licence: muscle jerks (myoclonus) of brain origin only
Studies
Germany 1995 (39 people with sudden hearing loss and new tinnitus; piracetam vs naftidrofuryl, both with infusions) · Greece 2004 (108 men with tinnitus after noise injury; 4 randomized drug groups) · India 2021 (non-randomized; see above) · Hungary 2025 (1 case)
Comparator
Other medicines — no placebo
Tinnitus endpoint
🔉 Loudness in decibels (1995); questionnaire and VAS (2004)
Result
No difference from the comparison medicines in either randomized study (1995: 27 vs 19.9 dB reduction, not significant)
Limitations
Small, recent-onset populations where natural recovery is common; no placebo
Regulatory status (by country)
  • United States — vinpocetine: the FDA tentatively concluded in 2016 that vinpocetine does not meet the definition of a dietary ingredient (no final decision found), and in June 2019 warned women who are or could become pregnant not to take it. No FDA-approved vinpocetine drug was found.
  • United States — piracetam: no FDA approval found. In a 2019 warning letter to one seller, the FDA said the piracetam products it reviewed were not dietary supplements (based on the website’s claims).
  • United Kingdom — piracetam (Nootropil): authorised as an add-on treatment for myoclonus of cortical origin; no hearing or tinnitus indication.
  • Russia — Cavinton: the product information (reproduced on Vidal.ru; the official state register could not be accessed) lists the sensation of noise in the ears among its approved uses, and also lists tinnitus as a rare side effect.
  • Hungary — Cavinton Forte: authorised with tinnitus among its ENT indications; a 2023 national health-technology assessment notes that other European vinpocetine products carry only neurological indications.
  • Japan — vinpocetine: a generic was discontinued and recalled in August 2001 after a placebo-controlled re-evaluation trial could not confirm efficacy for its approved use (symptoms of reduced brain blood flow after stroke — not tinnitus).
best: Pilgramm M, Schumann K, 1986 — HNO (Germany): 8 studies, 400 soldiers after acute noise injury, some randomized and double-blind, with a saline control; vinpocetine given as an add-on to infusions
Hahn A, et al., 2008 — International Tinnitus Journal (Czech Republic): 150 people, 7 groups (54 given vinpocetine), 10 days, daily 0–10 rating; no placebo
Markou K, et al., 2004 (Greece): 108 men with tinnitus after acute noise injury, 4 randomized drug groups, questionnaire and VAS at 15 and 45 days; no placebo
Gutmann R, Mees K, 1995 (Germany): 39 people with sudden hearing loss and tinnitus; piracetam vs naftidrofuryl
None found for any of these studies
Peer-reviewed; abstracts read (German, Polish and Russian full texts not accessible); the 2008 Czech paper read in full

found.plain: No study shows either drug doing better than placebo for tinnitus. Adding vinpocetine to treatment after noise injury gave no extra benefit, and piracetam did no better than the other medicines it was compared with.
numbers: Vinpocetine, acute noise injury (1986): all active treatments beat saline, but vasoactive add-ons including vinpocetine did not improve results beyond infusions alone.

Vinpocetine, chronic tinnitus (2008): vinpocetine with physiotherapy was judged “most effective” of 7 groups, with no statistical comparison; the authors noted no treatment had an objective correlate.
🔉 Piracetam (1995): tinnitus reduction 27 dB vs 19.9 dB with naftidrofuryl — not significant.
Piracetam (2004): “no significant differences” between the four groups.

limits: No placebo-controlled tinnitus trial of either drug was found.
Most studies were in acute tinnitus after sudden hearing loss or noise injury, where natural recovery is common.
Vinpocetine was usually one of several treatments, often given together with other drugs or physiotherapy.
Outcomes were mostly simple ratings or “improvement,” not validated questionnaires.
Russian and Chinese databases could only be partly searched, so studies may have been missed.
vinpocetine.repl: Not applicable — there is no positive placebo-controlled result to repeat for either drug.
vinpocetine.safety:
• Regulatory warning (US FDA, 2019) — vinpocetine: may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development; not to be taken by women who are or could become pregnant. Based on animal studies showing fetal loss and heart defects.
  • Regulatory label (Russia) — vinpocetine: not for use in pregnancy or breastfeeding; rare side effects include heart rhythm problems and tinnitus.
  • Regulatory label (UK) — piracetam: not for people with severe kidney disease or brain haemorrhage; caution with bleeding risk or blood thinners (including low-dose aspirin); dose reduction in kidney impairment.
  • Product quality (published analyses): both substances have been found in US products sold as supplements.
vinpocetine.guide:
Guidelines disagree, and none names piracetam.

For vinpocetine (archived)

Russia (2016; archived by the Russian Ministry of Health in May 2021 because its validity period expired — no current Russian tinnitus guideline was found): recommended vinpocetine, with other blood-flow drugs, for suspected blood-flow-related (“angiogenic”) inner-ear disorders — at its lowest grade (C, expert consensus).

Against drugs for tinnitus in general

Europe (2019): “weak recommendation against” drug treatment; no drug can generally be recommended. Germany (2021): drugs for chronic tinnitus are “to be avoided” (strong). Neither names vinpocetine or piracetam, so these are general statements. Japan (2019): drug treatment aimed at the tinnitus itself is not appropriate, though the same chapter calls blood-flow drugs promising. NICE (2020), Korea (2026): no statement.
vinpocetine.com: No commercial funding, drug supply or company authorship was documented for any tinnitus study of either drug. Gedeon Richter (Cavinton) and UCB (Nootropil) market the drugs; neither is recorded as involved in these studies.
vinpocetine.underway: No registered tinnitus trial of vinpocetine or piracetam was found in our search (ClinicalTrials.gov, EU registers, ISRCTN). The Chinese, Iranian and Indian registries could not be searched.
vinpocetine.why: Neither drug has been tested against placebo for tinnitus in any study found. Vinpocetine studies were mostly open, and adding it after noise injury gave no benefit; piracetam did no better than other medicines in two small studies. The only guideline recommending vinpocetine has been archived.
vinpocetine.cov: PubMed, Europe PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov, EU registers, ISRCTN, regulator websites (FDA, UK EMC, Hungary, Japan) and Russian, Chinese, Hungarian and Polish sources were searched. Russian databases (eLibrary, CyberLeninka), the Russian drug register, Chinese databases and the Iranian and Chinese registries were largely inaccessible. How this entry was corrected: piracetam has 2 randomized studies, not 3; one vinpocetine programme had a saline control; the Russian guideline was archived in 2021.

iran-herbal.special:
Four products, four evidence streams
1 · Neurotec capsule controlled, not yet confirmed
Ingredients
Dry extracts of tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) 62 mg, nettle (Urtica dioica) 30 mg and rose hip (Rosa canina) 8 mg per 100-mg capsule (current label; the trial paper does not give amounts)
Maker
Named differently across sources and years (ParsRoos, Nano Hayat, Rose Pharmed, Arvand Pharmed); how these relate could not be confirmed (Iran’s drug registry was not reachable)
Trial
Khosravi et al. 2023: 150 randomized, 103 analysed; 100 mg twice a day for 3 months vs placebo supplied by the manufacturer; described as double-blind
Tinnitus type
Chronic subjective tinnitus for 6 months or more
Result
At 3 months: 🧠 THI 37.5 vs 49.7 (P = 0.017) and all six rating scales lower, including 🔉 loudness (P = 0.043). No difference at 1 month. Hearing unchanged (a registered main outcome)
Limitations
31% not analysed; the Neurotec group started with worse scores and this was not adjusted for; several outcomes tested without correction; registered after recruitment ended; side effects not reported although registered; numbers read from the preprint because the journal version could not be accessed
2 · Nanocurcumin (Sina Curcumin) no benefit shown · 1 small trial
Dose
80 mg a day (high-absorption nano-micelle form) for 21 days
Trial
Farahani et al. 2022: 62 people, randomized, triple-blind, placebo capsules
Result
🧠 THI (the registered main outcome) 41.2 → 33.8 vs 39.2 → 37.2; no difference between groups at the end (P = 0.67). 🔉 Matched loudness and pitch no different. One comparison of score changes (P = 0.02) is reported inconsistently in the paper. The authors concluded it was “not effective”
Second trial
Tehran, 60 planned, 3 months: recruitment complete since 2019; no results found
3 · Herbal tea (Birjand) controlled, not yet confirmed (weak)
Ingredients
Salvia hydrangea, bitter-orange blossom, lemon verbena and elm bark, as a tea three times a day for 28–56 days
Trial
Karimi et al. 2019: 144 randomized to tea, cinnarizine or placebo capsules; single-blind
Result
🧠 THI at 56 days: 32.0 (tea) vs 31.2 (cinnarizine) vs 38.5 (placebo) — tea better than placebo only at 56 days. Severity rating no different
Limitations
A tea cannot be blinded against a capsule our interpretation; six people whose tinnitus resolved were excluded from the analysis; registered after the trial; side effects claimed absent without data
4 · Bitter almond oil ear drops no benefit shown · 1 trial
Product
Barij Essence ear drops, 2 drops twice a day, added to cinnarizine for 4 weeks
Trial
Arabi et al. 2025: 69 people, randomized, open-label — no placebo
Result
No difference between groups on the registered main measure (severity rating) or on THI

These are different products. A result for one says nothing about the others. our interpretation

The two positive trials have serious weaknesses: high dropout and unadjusted baseline differences (Neurotec); unmatched placebo and exclusion of people who improved (tea).
Both positive trials were registered only after they had run.
Several outcomes were tested without correction for multiple comparisons.

iran-herbal.repl: No independent repeat of any of the four products was found in our search. A 2025 systematic review of plant extracts (English-language studies only) concluded that the extracts it included, among them Neurotec, showed no significant effect.
iran-herbal.safety:
• Randomized-trial adverse events: none in either group in the nanocurcumin trial; not reported in the Neurotec trial (although registered as an outcome); the tea trial claims no side effects without showing data.
  • Regulatory action (Italy, 2019) and government health information (US NIH NCCIH): a cluster of liver-injury reports led to regulatory action on turmeric supplements; NCCIH says highly bioavailable curcumin formulations may harm the liver. Nanocurcumin is a high-bioavailability form our interpretation.
  • Pharmacological concern (European Medicines Agency): tansy contains thujone, which the EMA treats as toxic to the nervous system at high enough doses and advises minimising in pregnancy and children; it says the thujone content of herbal medicines should be specified. We found no thujone figure for Neurotec in the maker’s information or in any published analysis; thujone levels in tansy and tansy extracts vary widely between plants and growing sites.
  • Pharmacological concern: bitter almond seeds contain amygdalin, which can release cyanide. The maker’s page for its bitter almond oil lists fatty acids as the active ingredients and gives skin use only; it mentions tests for microbes, heavy metals and pesticides but not for amygdalin or cyanide. The trial registry and summary do not say how the ear drops were made or tested.
  • Nettle (EMA monograph): stomach upset and allergic skin reactions.
iran-herbal.guide: No treatment-specific guideline position found. None of these products is named in any guideline we checked. The German (2021) guideline says food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus,” and its supporting text mentions phytotherapeutics; the European (2019) guideline recommends against dietary supplements. These broad statements may cover capsule products sold as supplements, but not clearly the tea or the ear drops, and Neurotec is described both as a medicine and as a supplement — so we do not apply them as a position on this card. NICE (2020), Japan (2019) and Korea (2026) have no relevant statement.
iran-herbal.com:
• Neurotec: “Placebo capsules were provided by … the Neurotec manufacturer” (trial preprint). The trial was funded by the university. The first author is affiliated with a private research consultancy; no link to the manufacturer is documented.
  • Nanocurcumin: university-funded (Hamadan); the authors declare no conflict of interest; no manufacturer role documented.
  • Herbal tea: university grant; prepared by a named individual; no conflict of interest declared.
  • Almond ear drops: a Barij Essence product; university-funded; the full text was not read.

Product supply does not by itself make a study’s results wrong.
iran-herbal.underway: No active or upcoming trial of these products for tinnitus was found in our search.
iran-herbal.why: Each product has been tested only once. The two positive trials had high dropout, an unmatched placebo or exclusions of people who improved, and both were registered after they ran; the two other products showed no benefit.
iran-herbal.cov: PubMed, Europe PMC, ClinicalTrials.gov, the Iranian trial registry (English and Persian), OpenAlex, Crossref and Persian web sources were searched. SID, Magiran and Iran’s drug registry could not be reached, and the journal version of the Neurotec trial was not accessible. homeopathy.safety:
• Trials: no adverse events reported (absence of reporting is not evidence of safety).

homeopathy.guide:
Guideline recommends against use — European (2019) and German (2021) guidelines. The European guideline gives a “Recommendation against” dietary and alternative therapies; homeopathy is named in the supporting text of that section, among therapies for which evidence of efficacy “does not exist.” The German guideline says food supplements “are to be omitted for chronic tinnitus” (strong recommendation) and names homeopathy in its supporting text. (Wording checked against the guideline texts.)

NICE (2020), Japan (2019) and Korea (2026) take no position on homeopathy. Whether the AAO-HNSF (2014) full text names homeopathy could not be checked, so it is not cited. The archived Russian guideline (2016) only listed homeopathic remedies among treatments in use.
homeopathy.com:

peptides.claimed: Online sellers and some clinics describe these peptides as “healing,” “regenerative,” “anti-inflammatory” or supporting “nerve repair,” and some promote them for tinnitus. These are marketing or mechanism descriptions, not evidence of benefit for tinnitus.

studied.title: People with tinnitus
studied.text: No study testing any of the four peptides on its own in people with tinnitus was found. One Russian report gave Semax together with four other treatments (see below).

studied.title: People with hearing loss
studied.text: No hearing study of any of the four was found; two Russian articles mention Semax among drugs used for hearing loss, without data.

studied.title: Animals
studied.text: No animal study of the ear, hearing or tinnitus-like behaviour was found for any of the four. Studies of related molecules (erythropoietin for the ear; ACTH fragments for balance) concern different compounds and do not transfer.

studied.title: Laboratory and other conditions
studied.text: Extensive laboratory and animal work in other tissues (mainly BPC-157 and Semax), and small human trials in other conditions (ARA-290 in nerve pain; Semax in stroke; Selank in anxiety).

peptides.special:
Four peptides, four separate stories
BPC-157 no ear evidence
What it is
A 15-amino-acid peptide described as a fragment of a gastric-juice protein. FDA’s 2026 review says its molecular targets “have not been identified”
Status (US)
Not approved in any country (FDA review, May 2026). Listed on FDA’s compounding safety-risk page under substances “nominated but withdrawn” (page dated 22 April 2026). FDA staff recommended against allowing pharmacies to compound it. On 23 July 2026 an FDA advisory committee voted narrowly in favour: 8 for, 6 against, 1 abstaining, in separate votes on the free-base and acetate forms, with the same result each time (FDA’s recorded webcast; FDA had not posted written minutes when we checked in September 2026). The vote is advisory: FDA would still have to go through formal rulemaking, and we found no final FDA decision.
Anti-doping
Named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List (section S0, non-approved substances)
Human studies
One ulcerative-colitis enema trial (no significant difference from placebo, per FDA) and small uncontrolled case series in other conditions
Ear, hearing or tinnitus
None found (a 2026 rat study with the ear drug gentamicin measured the kidneys only)
ARA-290 (cibinetide) no ear evidence
What it is
An 11-amino-acid peptide engineered from part of erythropoietin, designed not to raise red-cell counts
Status
Investigational. EU orphan designations for sarcoidosis (2013) and pancreatic-islet transplantation (2016) (EMA). US orphan-drug designations (FDA database, listed under the chemical name): sarcoidosis (2016) and neuropathic pain in sarcoidosis (2011) — designations, not approvals
Anti-doping
Not named; belongs to a class WADA prohibits (innate repair receptor agonists) our interpretation
Human studies
Small placebo-controlled trials in nerve pain from sarcoidosis and diabetes — different conditions
Ear, hearing or tinnitus
None found
Semax no evidence for Semax alone
What it is
A 7-amino-acid analogue of an ACTH fragment
Status
Russia: licensed prescription medicine (Peptogen) for cognitive problems in cerebrovascular disease, stroke recovery and optic-nerve disease — no hearing indication (label reproduced on Russian drug-reference sites; the state register could not be accessed). US: not approved; on the same FDA page as BPC-157; FDA staff recommended against compounding; an FDA advisory committee voted in favour on 24 July 2026: 8 for, 5 against, 1 abstaining, the same in separate votes on the free-base and acetate forms (FDA’s recorded webcast; no written minutes posted yet). The vote is advisory and there is no final FDA decision.

Tinnitus

Online “research chemical” products are unregulated in the US; their content and purity are not controlled (FDA warning letters to sellers) our interpretation.
Russian databases (eLibrary) and the Russian drug and trial registers could not be accessed.
peptides.repl: Not applicable — there is no tinnitus result to repeat.
peptides.safety:
• Regulatory statements (US FDA): FDA says it lacks sufficient information to know whether BPC-157 or Semax “would cause harm” when given to people, noting possible immune reactions and impurities; for Semax, FDA also notes a possible bleeding risk. FDA adverse-event reports for BPC-157 include injection-site reactions and skin darkening; whether BPC-157 caused them is unclear.

  • Randomized-trial adverse events: ARA-290 sarcoidosis trial — serious adverse events in a few people on the drug and none on placebo; no ear-related events listed.

peptides.guide: No treatment-specific guideline position found. None of the four peptides is named in the European (2019), German (2021), NICE (2020), Japanese (2019) or Korean (2026) guidelines. peptides.underway: No registered tinnitus or hearing trial of any of the four peptides was found in our search. Registered BPC-157 trials concern healthy volunteers, muscle and tendon injuries.
peptides.why: None of these peptides has been tested in people with tinnitus, and none has animal ear research. The one report involving Semax combined it with four other treatments. Their appeal rests on general “healing” claims and laboratory work in other tissues.

chips: No independent repeat of the withdrawal design
caffeine.claimed: Cutting out coffee, tea and other caffeine is one of the most common pieces of advice given to people with tinnitus, on the idea that caffeine is a stimulant that makes tinnitus louder. It is free advice rather than a product, and it is repeated on many health and hearing websites. Tinnitus UK (a charity) says there is “no scientific basis for this advice.”

studied.title: People with tinnitus — reducing caffeine
studied.text: 1 double-blind crossover trial (66 people, habitual drinkers): no difference between caffeinated and decaffeinated days. 1 uncontrolled study (26 enrolled, 22 analysed): scores fell over 30 days with no comparison group.

studied.title: People with tinnitus — one caffeine dose
studied.text: 1 randomized, triple-blind trial (80 people): one 300 mg dose did not change tinnitus measures compared with placebo 1 hour later. This tests an immediate effect, not cutting down.

studied.title: Population studies (not treatment)
studied.text: Large cohort and survey studies (for example 65,085 US nurses followed for 18 years; UK Biobank) found no link or slightly less new tinnitus with higher caffeine intake. These are associations: they cannot show that caffeine prevents or causes tinnitus.

caffeine.special:
Three kinds of caffeine evidence, kept apart
Cutting down (the actual advice) no benefit shown
Controlled trial
St Claire et al. 2010: habitual drinkers’ usual tea and coffee replaced by blinded caffeinated or decaffeinated supplies for 30 days, with phased withdrawal; no difference in Tinnitus Questionnaire scores
Uncontrolled study
Figueiredo et al. 2014: asked to cut coffee by at least half for 30 days; the 22 who managed it had lower THI scores afterwards, but there was no comparison group and those who did not cut down were excluded
One dose (an immediate effect) no effect
Controlled trial
Ledesma et al. 2021: 300 mg caffeine vs placebo capsule after 24 hours without caffeine; THI fell in both groups, with no difference between them. Participants drank little caffeine (about 92 mg a day)
Population studies (prevention / association) association only
Findings
No link, or less new tinnitus with more caffeine (Nurses’ Health Study II; UK Biobank; Korean and Italian studies). Decaffeinated coffee showed no association
What this cannot show
That drinking caffeine prevents tinnitus — people who drink more caffeine may differ in other ways, and people with tinnitus may cut down on advice

found.plain: Cutting out caffeine made no measurable difference to tinnitus in the one double-blind trial, and people had withdrawal symptoms while cutting down.
numbers: Withdrawal trial: difference in Tinnitus Questionnaire score between caffeinated and decaffeinated days −0.04 points (95% CI −1.99 to 1.93) — a difference between conditions, with a narrow range on a 0–84 scale.
Withdrawal trial: “significant acute adverse symptoms of caffeine withdrawal were observed.”
Single-dose trial: no significant difference between caffeine and placebo in change on any questionnaire.
Uncontrolled study: average THI fell 10.2 points over 30 days in the 22 people analysed — a change within one group, without a comparison group, so it cannot be attributed to cutting caffeine.

limits: Only one trial tested cutting down, and it was small and short (about 2 weeks per condition).
Allocation was “pseudo-randomized,” and we could not read the full text to check dropouts or how many people were analysed.
Withdrawal symptoms in the early phase could have masked a later benefit; a benefit for some individuals cannot be ruled out.
The single-dose trial tested an immediate effect in light caffeine users, not cutting down.
The uncontrolled study excluded people who did not cut down, had no comparison group and differs from its registry record.
caffeine.repl: The withdrawal design has not been repeated. An independent single-dose trial in a different country also found no effect, but it asked a different question.
caffeine.safety:
• Observed in the withdrawal trial: significant short-term caffeine-withdrawal symptoms; the authors note withdrawal “might add to the burden of tinnitus.”
  • Pharmacological (general, not tinnitus-specific): stopping caffeine commonly causes headache and tiredness for 2–9 days, starting 12–24 hours after the last dose; cutting down gradually reduces this (review of withdrawal studies, Juliano & Griffiths 2004).
  • No serious harms from cutting down caffeine were reported in any tinnitus study.
caffeine.guide: No treatment-specific guideline recommendation found. The German (2021) guideline mentions, in background text citing a 2019 review, that reducing caffeine “had neither a positive nor a negative effect” — this is not a graded recommendation. The US (AAO-HNSF 2014) guideline mentions caffeine only as something to ask about when taking a history. The European (2019), UK (NICE 2020), Japanese (2019) and Korean (2026) guidelines do not mention caffeine. An archived 2016 Russian guideline listed caffeine as a stimulant for some patients (historical only).
caffeine.com:
• Withdrawal trial: funded by a grant from the charity Deafness Research UK, which had no role in the study’s design, analysis or writing; the authors declared no conflicts of interest (paper’s acknowledgements).
  • Single-dose trial: no specific funding; a private ear, nose and throat institute where recruitment took place is listed as a supporting source in the registry.
  • No coffee- or decaf-industry funding was found for any tinnitus caffeine study; none is assumed.
caffeine.underway: No registered trial of cutting down caffeine for tinnitus is under way in our search. The two registry records below belong to studies that have already been published.
caffeine.why: Cutting out caffeine has been tested once in a double-blind trial, which found no difference. That trial was small and short, so a benefit for some individuals cannot be ruled out, but there is no evidence that giving up caffeine helps tinnitus on average — and stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms.
caffeine.cov: PubMed, Europe PMC, Crossref, ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN, the Iranian and Brazilian registries, guideline texts, and Chinese, Korean, Portuguese, German and Persian search terms were used. The withdrawal trial’s full text, the Australian and Chinese registries, and Chinese and Korean databases could not be searched directly. How this entry was corrected: the first author is St Claire; the trial compared caffeinated and decaffeinated days within one 30-day crossover (not two 30-day groups); the German guideline sentence is background text, not a recommendation.

found.plain: Tinnitus scores fell in all three groups, including placebo. The medicine groups did not improve significantly more than placebo, and when everyone randomized was counted, no group changed significantly.
numbers: Between groups (main comparison): P = 0.265 among completers; P = 0.590 counting everyone randomized.
Difference from placebo: about −6 TFI points, 95% CI about −15 to +3 — Tinnitus Evidence calculation. The range includes no effect and a modest effect.

Responders (fall of 13 or more points): 42% and 41% vs 23% — a threshold for individual change, not a difference between group averages. A fall of about 13 TFI points is a threshold for change noticed by an individual patient. It is not a threshold for a difference between group averages, so the two should not be compared directly.
Dropouts: 4 of 23 and 6 of 28 on the medicines vs 1 of 27 on placebo.

limits: One small, short, single-centre trial with no power calculation.
The main analysis counted only people who finished, and more people dropped out of the medicine groups.
Registered after the trial began, so earlier changes to its plan cannot be ruled out.
Most participants did not have migraine, so it does not test the “cochlear migraine” idea directly; migraine history did not predict response in a follow-up analysis.
Side effects occurred only in the medicine groups, which could reveal who was on active treatment; blinding was not checked.
The authors’ positive wording relies on changes within each group, not on the comparison with placebo.
migraine-protocols.repl: No independent trial of these combinations was found. The two registered follow-on trials have no placebo group, and one is open-label.
migraine-protocols.safety:
• Observed in the trial (8 weeks): no serious side effects. 4 people on the medicines stopped because of side effects (stomach pain, tiredness, erectile dysfunction, blurred vision), none on placebo. Taste change, dry mouth and trouble sleeping were also reported. The side-effect lists differ between the paper, the registry and a follow-up paper.
  • Regulatory warnings (US FDA labels of the individual medicines): nortriptyline and paroxetine carry boxed warnings about suicidal thoughts in children, teenagers and young adults; topiramate labels warn of eye problems (acute glaucoma), metabolic acidosis and harm in pregnancy; verapamil labels warn of low blood pressure and heart failure.
  • Longer-term use for tinnitus has not been studied.
migraine-protocols.guide: Class-level positions only — no guideline names these protocols. The US (AAO-HNSF 2014) guideline recommends against antidepressants and anticonvulsants for routine treatment of persistent, bothersome tinnitus; this covers nortriptyline, paroxetine and topiramate but not verapamil. The European (2019) guideline says antidepressants should not be prescribed for tinnitus without a diagnosis of depression. The German (2021) guideline states that drugs for chronic tinnitus are “to be avoided” (strong recommendation). The Japanese (2019) guideline judges drug therapy aimed at tinnitus itself not appropriate. The UK (NICE 2020) and Korean (2026) guidelines take no position on these medicines.
migraine-protocols.com:
• Disclosure in the trial publication: the senior author “is an advisor and holds equity in NeuroMed Care LLC, Elinava Technologies, and Cactus Medical LLC.”
  • Clinic marketing: NeuroMed Care’s pages, written by the same doctor (described there as its Chief Medical Advisor), promote this approach with success figures; the price of its programme is not shown.
  • Disclosures vary: this author’s financial disclosures differ between papers (some list NeuroMed, others do not).
  • The medicines are generic; no patent was found in a web search.
migraine-protocols.underway: Two registered trials are listed as active; neither has a placebo group, so neither can confirm a benefit over placebo. The Stanford trial compares newer anti-CGRP migraine drugs with older ones, openly, in people with migraine.
migraine-protocols.why: The only placebo-controlled trial did not show that these medicine combinations work better than placebo. It was small and short, so a modest effect cannot be ruled out, but the positive claims rest on improvements within groups — and placebo improved too.

The Chinese, Japanese and Australian registries and the ClinicalTrials.gov version history could not be accessed. How this entry was corrected: 1 trial (78 people), not 2 studies (140); the trial did not select people with migraine; side effects are now extracted; comparisons of group averages with the individual 13-point threshold were removed.

ear-seeds.claimed: Ear-seed kits (small Vaccaria seeds or beads on tape) and magnetic ear clips are sold online for tinnitus; one clip listing promises to “Stop Ear Ringing.” In China, ear seeds (耳穴压豆) are a routine hospital nursing technique. A US ear-seed seller’s tinnitus article cites a study that actually tested a clamp worn behind the ear, not ear seeds.

studied.title: People with tinnitus — ear seeds
studied.text: At least 21 randomized trials added ear seeds to another treatment and compared that with the other treatment alone (about 1,900 people), and at least 30 more combined seeds with other extra treatments. All were unblinded; none used a sham. A 2026 Chinese review counted 61 papers.

studied.title: People with tinnitus — magnets
studied.text: Magnetic ear pellets: 3 small Chinese studies, always combined with other treatments; no study compared magnetic with non-magnetic beads. Consumer magnetic ear clips: no studies found.

studied.title: People with sudden hearing loss
studied.text: Several trials enrolled people with sudden hearing loss, where hearing and tinnitus often improve on their own. These are counted separately from chronic tinnitus.

found.plain: Almost every trial reports that adding ear seeds helped. Because none used a sham and nearly all were unblinded, these results cannot separate the seeds from expectation, extra attention or natural improvement.
numbers: 2019 Shanghai thesis: “effective rate” 79% with ear seeds vs 61% with counselling and sound therapy alone — a composite measure, not a validated tinnitus score.
A 2018 trial (83 people, sound masking with or without seeds): THI after treatment about 10 vs 19 points — end-of-treatment averages, not changes, and not blinded.
No trial reported results after treatment stopped.

limits: No sham-controlled trial of ear seeds alone was found in any language or registry we could search.
Nearly all trials were unblinded, and many used composite “effective rates” or traditional symptom scores rather than validated tinnitus questionnaires.
Many enrolled people with sudden hearing loss or very recent tinnitus, which often improves on its own.
Almost all results are positive, which suggests publication bias our interpretation.
Most Chinese studies were read only as abstracts; several show internal inconsistencies, such as studies described as both retrospective and randomized.
ear-seeds.repl: Many different hospitals report similar add-on results, but no result has been tested against a sham, so independent replication of a specific effect is unclear.
ear-seeds.safety:
• Systematic review of auricular therapy (other conditions): side effects of ear acupressure were local skin irritation, discomfort, mild tenderness or pain, and dizziness; mostly short-lived, with no serious adverse events.
  • Observed in tinnitus trials: most abstracts report no adverse events; trials excluded people with ear-skin damage or adhesive allergy.
  • Magnets (our interpretation): no tinnitus-specific safety data were found. People with cochlear implants, pacemakers or other implanted devices should not place magnets near them without advice — a precaution, not a documented harm.
  • Indirect: sudden hearing loss with tinnitus needs prompt medical assessment; in the trials, seeds were always added to standard care.
ear-seeds.guide: No guideline position on ear seeds, acupressure or ear magnets. The German (2021) guideline says “(Electro)acupuncture should not be practiced for chronic tinnitus” — this concerns needle and electro-acupuncture and is not applied here. The European (2019) and US (2014) guidelines make no recommendation about acupuncture; the Japanese (2019) guideline says no alternative therapy can currently be recommended, discussing needle acupuncture. The UK (NICE 2020) and Korean (2026) guidelines do not mention acupressure.
ear-seeds.com:
• Products: ear-seed kits and magnetic ear clips are widely sold online; listings for clips claim tinnitus relief. Sellers are not named.
  • Misattributed evidence: one ear-seed seller’s tinnitus article cites a 2021 study that tested a clamp worn behind the ear (made by a company that donated the data; the lead author disclosed paid consultancy), not ear seeds.
  • Funding was rarely stated in the Chinese trials; no manufacturer funding was documented.
ear-seeds.underway: The Taiwan trial is the only registered sham-controlled trial found. It bundles magnetic-bead ear acupressure with ear nerve stimulation, so it cannot show the effect of ear seeds alone. Several Chinese registry records appeared in web searches but could not be opened.
ear-seeds.why: Many trials have been published, but none has compared ear seeds with a sham, so it is unknown whether the seeds do anything beyond expectation, extra care or natural recovery. Magnetic clips have not been studied at all.

ozone.repl: Not applicable for benefit — both controlled trials found no difference, and no positive controlled result exists to repeat.
ozone.safety:
• Regulatory statement (US federal regulation, 21 CFR 801.415): ozone is “a toxic gas with no known useful medical application”; inhaled ozone irritates the lungs.
  • Regulatory action (US FDA, 2025): warning letter to a maker of ozone blood-treatment devices marketed without approval.
  • Case reports (ozone blood treatment and injections, not tinnitus-specific): a fatal gas embolism; gas embolism in the brain causing temporary blindness; stroke; a heart attack; and a hepatitis C outbreak among patients of one clinic.
  • Review of autohaemotherapy harms (2026): haemolysis, kidney failure, allergic reactions and infection are reported, but how often they occur cannot be reliably estimated.
  • Tinnitus studies: no side effects were reported in the small studies that described them — too few people to detect rare harms.
ozone.guide: No guideline position found. None of the guidelines checked — European (2019), German (2021), UK (NICE 2020), Japanese (2019), Korean (2026), and the archived Russian (2016) guideline — mentions ozone therapy. General statements against drug treatment for tinnitus are not applied to ozone.
ozone.com:
• Main trial: funded by a university research fund (not commercial).
  • Cuban studies: the research centre that published them also makes and supplies ozone equipment (stated in a related paper); no conflict of interest was declared.
  • Devices: an ear-insufflation device sold online lists tinnitus among its uses. Clinics offering ozone for tinnitus exist in several countries; they are not named.
ozone.underway: No registered trial of ozone therapy for tinnitus, hearing loss or Ménière’s disease was found in the registries we could search.
ozone.why: Both small controlled trials found no benefit, and the positive reports have no comparison group. Ozone blood treatments carry rare but serious risks, including gas embolism.

ketamine.safety:

ketamine.guide: No treatment-specific guideline position found for ketamine or esketamine in tinnitus. kv7.special:
Prevention versus treatment
What the animal studies tested

Loud noise → drug given within 30 minutes to 1 week → tinnitus-like behaviour tested 1–5 weeks later. In none of these studies was tinnitus confirmed before the drug was given. This is prevention.

What people with tinnitus usually need

Treatment of tinnitus that is already established. Not tested in any animal or human study of these drugs found in our search — except the small flupirtine study, which found no benefit.

Five evidence streams
Retigabine (ezogabine)
Animal
Mice: tinnitus-like behaviour prevented when given from 30 minutes, or from day 3, after noise
Human
Only an online self-report survey (53 users; no control)
Regulatory
Approved 2011 (US, EU) for epilepsy; US boxed warning and EU restriction (2013) for retinal and skin pigmentation; discontinued worldwide by the maker in 2017 for “very limited usage,” “not due to efficacy or safety reasons”; EU authorisation withdrawn at the company’s request (19 July 2018)
Flupirtine 1 human study, no benefit
Human
Salembier et al. 2006: open, single group, 24 people, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks — no effect on loudness (VAS) or distress (Tinnitus Questionnaire); one person improved but stopped because of memory and concentration problems. Not replicated. 30 anecdotal case reports (German congress report, 2000)
Animal
10 mice pooled with retigabine in a prevention study
Regulatory
EU: medicines withdrawn in 2018 because of the risk of serious liver injury (EMA PRAC recommendation, CMDh consensus, March 2018)
Azetukalner (XEN1101)
Status
Phase 3 in epilepsy; trials in depression. Not approved anywhere; no tinnitus trial or animal tinnitus study found
Opakalim (BHV-7000)
Status
Phase 2/3 in epilepsy; some trials completed or stopped. Not approved; no tinnitus trial found. (The same company has a separate preclinical tinnitus program with a different drug, intranasal oxytocin.)
Laboratory Kv7 compounds
Studies
SF0034 and RL-81 (mice, prevention or early treatment after noise, one laboratory); in rats, a Kv7-opening compound and its mirror-image form that dampens Kv7 channels both suppressed aspirin-induced tinnitus-like behaviour — so the mechanism is not settled

AC102 is not a Kv7 drug; it has its own card.

Procedure by procedure

These procedures differ in target, method, risk and evidence. Their results are shown separately and are not averaged.

1 · Pulsed radiofrequency of nerves in the upper neck and around the ear most studied
Targets
C2 nerve root ganglion; the ear branch of the vagus nerve; the auriculotemporal nerve (in front of the ear); neck facet nerves; the greater occipital nerve
Rationale
Pulsed electrical current is proposed to change nerve signalling without destroying the nerve
Studies
About 11 reports: 6 from one Dutch clinic (61, 112 and 67 people, plus cases), 1 independent Turkish series (22 people) and case reports
Control / sham
None
Tinnitus subtype
Mostly any tinnitus (the Dutch series had no exclusion criteria)
Results
🔉 25–48% reported lower loudness at 7 weeks in the Dutch series (4-point patient rating). 🧠 Independent series: THI 42 → 37 at 1 month, not significant; 1 of 22 improved by half or more
Worse
3–4% reported worse tinnitus in the Dutch series
Limitations
Retrospective, non-standard rating by telephone, single clinic; the only independent series was negative
2 · Radiofrequency lesion of the superior cervical sympathetic ganglion
Target
A sympathetic nerve ganglion high in the neck — not the stellate ganglion
Rationale
Proposed sympathetic-nervous-system involvement in tinnitus
Studies
1 retrospective Dutch series (2016); 1 Iranian randomized trial vs cinnarizine (40 planned) — recruitment complete, no results found
Control / sham
None (the Iranian trial compares with tablets, not a sham)
Results
64% reported relief at 7 weeks — but only people who first responded to a test injection received the procedure
Limitations
Selected responders; number treated not given in the abstract; permanent nerve lesion
3 · Nerve blocks with local anaesthetic (sometimes with a steroid) best reported: 30-person prospective series
Targets
Greater occipital nerve (back of the head); cervical plexus; neck nerve roots; face and ear nerves; a nerve cluster reached from inside the mouth; neck epidural space
Rationale
Numbing nerves that may feed into hearing pathways
Studies
About 13 reports: occipital-nerve blocks (Japan 1970s; 28 people in 1999; a clinic series of 147 combined with trigger-point injections); cervical plexus block in whiplash-related tinnitus (30 people, UK NHS, 2024); 4 neck nerve-root series from the Dutch clinic (248 people); face and ear nerve blocks (55 people, Korea); intra-oral injections (19 people, Germany); single cases

None

Often people with neck pain, whiplash or neck tenderness

14 of 28 improved after occipital-nerve blocks; 23 of 30 (77%) reported a meaningful drop in loudness at 3 months and 19 of 30 (63%) at 6 months after cervical plexus block; 18–30% responded after neck nerve-root injections
Limitations
Uncontrolled; different measures; steroids often given at the same time
4 · Trigger-point injections
Studies
No injection-only tinnitus study found; they appear only combined with nerve blocks or other treatments

rf-nerve-blocks.safety:
• Documented procedural risk (review of published cases): after steroid injections near nerve roots in the neck (cervical transforaminal injections), serious complications including 13 deaths and 31 brain or spinal cord infarctions have been reported, mostly with particulate steroids. This applies to that procedure family. The tinnitus series injected at this site (the cervical nerve-root openings) with dexamethasone, a non-particulate steroid; the review advises non-particulate steroids for cervical procedures.
  • Case series: 3–5% reported worse tinnitus after radiofrequency or nerve-root injections in the Dutch series; one person had dizziness. Transient facial weakness for 5–15 minutes was reported (and intended) with face-nerve blocks.
  • Known procedural risk (review): occipital-nerve blocks are mostly associated with minor effects such as fainting episodes; rare persistent hair loss at the injection site with steroid.
  • Pharmacological concern: local-anaesthetic toxicity can itself cause tinnitus (case reports).
  • No randomized-trial adverse-event data exist for any of these procedures.
rf-nerve-blocks.guide:
No treatment-specific guideline position found in the European (2019), German (2021), NICE (2020), Japanese (2019) or Korean (2026) guidelines. The German guideline’s general statement against drugs for chronic tinnitus does not name these procedures, and we do not apply it to them.

Russia (2016; archived by the Russian Ministry of Health in May 2021 because its validity period expired — no current Russian tinnitus guideline was found) recommended, at its lowest grade, interventions on the sympathetic ganglia of the neck when autonomic-nervous-system problems are established — not specific to radiofrequency or nerve blocks.
rf-nerve-blocks.com:
• No device-manufacturer funding was found for any study.
  • Dutch pain clinic: the clinician who wrote most of the radiofrequency and nerve-root series works at pain clinics offering these treatments; his papers declare no conflict of interest. A clinic website says it specialises in tinnitus and that its treatments are reimbursed.
  • Korean series: two of four authors are affiliated with a private pain clinic; no commercial relationship declared.
  • German pilot: patients were treated at the private ENT practice of a co-author.

A professional or clinic interest does not by itself make a study’s results wrong.
rf-nerve-blocks.why: Several different procedures share this card, and none has been compared with a sham procedure. Most radiofrequency results come from one clinic with a non-standard rating, and the first independent series found no benefit. The most carefully reported nerve-block study (30 people after whiplash) had no comparison group.

found.plain: MemoVigor 2 did better than placebo on a tinnitus handicap questionnaire (THI) after 3 months. The average difference from placebo was about 7.7 points. acamprosate.special:
Acamprosate trials at a glance
Acamprosate small positive trials, not confirmed
What it is
A drug licensed for alcohol dependence (US, UK); acts on glutamate and GABA signalling
Trials
Brazil 2005 (50 randomized, 41 analysed, 90 days); India 2012 (crossover, 40 analysed, 6 weeks per period); Iran 2020 (20 people, 30 days) — all placebo-controlled, oral, 333–666 mg three times a day. India 2023: open trial added to sound therapy (60 people)
Endpoints
Mostly a single “bother” rating or composite scores; THI in the Iranian trial
Findings
All published comparisons favoured acamprosate — for example 86.9% vs 44.4% improved (Brazil) and 92.5% vs 12.5% (India)
Limitations
