threshold-sound-conditioning.special:
Three different questions: hearing, tinnitus and regulation
Hearing evidence 1 small randomized trial — not tinnitus
Question
Do hearing thresholds change after 2–3 weeks of listening to threshold-level sound?
Evidence
One randomized trial by the method’s inventors reported more people with a change of 10 dB or more at some test frequency in the TSC group (78% vs 44%, as reported). The trial is small and reports differing control-group figures in two tables (see below). No independent replication was identified in our search.
Tinnitus evidence none identified in our search
Question
Does the method reduce tinnitus loudness or bother, and does any benefit last?
Evidence
No published human tinnitus study of TSC, REVE134, or Tinnitogram was identified in our search (28 September 2026). The hearing trial did not measure tinnitus. In our search, tinnitus-benefit claims in marketing could not be traced to a peer-reviewed publication or trial-registry record.
Regulatory status cleared as tinnitus sound generators
Question
What has the US FDA decided?
Decision
Two software programs were cleared through the 510(k) route as tinnitus maskers, for “temporary relief.” This is a finding of equivalence to earlier sound generators. The clearances do not establish that TSC improves tinnitus or produces durable benefit. Details in the next section.
Regulatory status (US FDA)
  • REVE134 — 510(k) K151719, KW Ear Lab, Inc.: “substantially equivalent” decision dated 9 October 2015; product code KLW (“Masker, Tinnitus”), 21 CFR 874.3400, Class II; prescription use. Cleared indication (quoted): “a sound generating software used in a Tinnitus Management Program designed to provide temporary relief for people experiencing tinnitus symptoms,” for use by hearing healthcare professionals, who should recommend listening “for 30 minutes twice a day at the barely audible level (minimally detectable level).” Performance data in the summary: software verification under IEC 62304 and ISO 14971, and an equivalence argument against Oticon Tinnitus SoundSupport (K133308) and GN Resound Tinnitus Sound Generator (K110932).
  • Tinnitogram Signal Generator — 510(k) K221168, Goldenear Company, Inc.: decision dated 1 February 2023; same product code and regulation; the only predicate is REVE134 (K151719); the cleared indication is near-identical. The FDA file states: “There was no clinical testing required to support the medical device as the indications for use is equivalent to the predicate device.”
  • What a 510(k) clearance is: FDA’s decision letters find the device “substantially equivalent (for the indications for use stated in the enclosure)” to a legally marketed predicate. FDA’s regulation defines a tinnitus masker as a device “intended to generate noise of sufficient intensity and bandwidth to mask ringing in the ears or internal head noises,” and sets one special control: patient labelling. Clearance is not FDA approval. These clearances do not establish that TSC improves tinnitus or produces durable benefit. our interpretation
  • Naming: no FDA record identified in our search (openFDA and the decision documents, 28 September 2026) uses the term “Threshold Sound Conditioning,” and neither applicant has another 510(k) in that database. The link between the method and the cleared programs comes from the developers’ materials and from shared inventors and companies (see Commercial involvement). The cleared instructions mention only listening at the “barely audible level.”
  • Other regulatory status: the FDA device registration and listing database was not searched directly. Non-US regulatory status was not investigated.
The hearing trial in detail
  • Who and what: adults with sensorineural hearing loss (at least one test frequency above 40 dB HL). 96 people were screened, 52 excluded and 2 dropped out before randomization; 42 were randomized and 39 analysed (23 TSC, 16 control; 3 excluded for reasons such as ear wax and unreliable responses). TSC group: a behind-the-ear hearing aid delivering TSC for 1 hour a day “at the lowest audible level (i.e., the hearing threshold level)” for 2–3 weeks, in one narrow frequency region (3, 4 or 6 kHz) matched to each person’s poorest threshold. Control group: an identical hearing aid without TSC. Hearing was measured at eight to nine frequencies in both ears, once before and once after.
  • Result as reported: people were grouped by whether any test frequency changed by 10 dB or more. Counting “ameliorated” plus “mixed” (some frequencies improved, some worsened), the TSC group had 18 of 23 (78%) and the control group 7 of 16 (44%); p = 0.008 and p = 0.0005 as reported by the authors (ANOVA with Scheffé post-hoc tests). Improvement without any 10 dB worsening: 10 of 23 (43%) vs 4 of 16 (25%). At least one frequency worsened by 10 dB or more in 11 of 23 (48%) TSC and 10 of 16 (63%) control participants (Table 2). The paper does not report how many decibels thresholds changed, at which frequencies, or whether the treated frequency region improved.
  • Control-group figures differ between two tables: Table 2 and the abstract give the control group 4 improved, 3 mixed, 2 no change and 7 worsened; the subject-level Table 1 gives 4, 0, 5 and 7. That changes the control “ameliorated or mixed” figure from 7 of 16 (44%) to 4 of 16 (25%). The TSC group is the same in both tables. The reason for the difference is not stated in the paper, and we did not find a published correction addressing it. our recount

threshold-sound-conditioning.why: No published human tinnitus study of TSC, REVE134, or Tinnitogram was identified in our search. The one randomized trial measured hearing thresholds only, is small and short, was run by the method’s inventors, and reports differing control-group figures in two of its tables. The FDA clearances of the related tinnitus programs rest on equivalence to earlier devices, not on tinnitus trial data, and do not establish that TSC improves tinnitus or produces durable benefit.
